title: Google’s hyper-personalized ‘Dreambeans’ feed is now free to test [U]
snippet: Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test. more…
fullText:
Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test.

Update 9/10: Google officially announced the broader availability today.

Personalized topics: This could be everything from places to explore, shows to watch, or a reminder of upcoming events.

Connected apps: Distilled information from the Google apps you select, including Calendar, Gmail, Photos, Search, YouTube, and now Gemini.

Original 8/28: Dreambeans is very much like a hyper-personalized Google Now or Discover feed. Like the Gemini app and AI Mode, it uses Google’s Personal Intelligence system to learn your interests by looking at your Gmail, Google Photos, Calendar, Workspace, Search history, and YouTube. During setup, you can choose which apps Dreambeans can access.

Workspace supplies ground-truth transaction data like receipts and upcoming flights

Photos provides the visual memories and insights about you and the people in your life

YouTube identifies your active hobbies

Search detects your budding interests

By combining all these unique signals, Dreambeans can proactively generate rich and highly customized daily visual stories.

The app suggests topics to explore, things to try, places to visit, and interesting events. New stories arrive every morning.

	

Instead of using stock imagery, each Dreambeans story is accompanied by Nano Banana 2-generated artwork that uses an illustrated style. For example, if Dreambeans recommends a hike, you might see yourself and a group of friends at that location.

Tapping on a story lets you see a longer description. In the same example, you’ll get trail details, specific places to stop, what to wear, and timing recommendations. Dreambeans will link to trail guide content on the web. There’s also an “Ask anything” chat experience to get more information.

You can leave feedback by tapping the heart or downvoting, while the chat interface allows you to provide more details. “Tune your feed” lets you tell Dreambeans what you “want more stories about” and what it should never show.

The name combines two ideas at the heart of the app. The “dream” is how the app works overnight to find meaning in the content overload across your connected apps. It then distills what it finds into “beans” – a fresh collection of stories brewed for you each morning.

In June, it was just available for Google AI Ultra subscribers, with Google expanding to AI Pro earlier this month. The setup process “requires up to a day to build your first set of stories.” 

It remains to be seen how Dreambeans will graduate from Google Labs. The experience it offers today is largely standalone, with Daily Brief in the Gemini app possibly benefiting from a more visual experience. 

Dreambeans is available on Android and iOS in the US.

title: iPhone Duo is no Apple Vision Pro
snippet: Look, no offense to Apple Vision Pro. I’m sure Apple Vision Pro is a very nice person. But iPhone Duo and Apple Vision Pro are not the same. There’s a take that the iPhone Duo may have the Apple Vision Pro problem. The idea is that due to its price and device-specific software, it may be a miss and not a hit. The two things are not the same. more…
fullText:
Look, no offense to Apple Vision Pro. I’m sure Apple Vision Pro is a very nice person. But iPhone Duo and Apple Vision Pro are not the same.

There’s a take that the iPhone Duo may have the Apple Vision Pro problem. The idea is that due to its price and device-specific software, it may be a miss and not a hit.  The two things are not the same.

iPhone Duo doesn’t suffer from Apple Vision Pro’s biggest challenges

The biggest problem with this view is that Apple Vision Pro doesn’t replace core devices. It can be a portable movie theater and a better viewport into gaming, and mixed reality experiences can be really moving.

Apple Vision Pro doesn’t replace your iPhone or your iPad. It’s an immersive world that can fit in a suitcase. Apple Vision Pro is mostly a stationary appliance. It’s not a small tablet that can fit in your pocket that you’ll use literally everywhere you go.

Then there’s price. iPhone Duo’s $1999 starting price is a lot, but it’s not as bad as we’d feared. People are willing to pay for premium smartphones. That’s just a result of how important phones are to modern life. 

Apple Vision Pro’s original $3,499 starting price was never very palatable. Now it starts at $3,699. You can almost buy two iPhone Duos. That’s iPhone Quattro money. 

Utility, portability, and affordability all feed into the biggest difference. Apple Vision Pro fails as a mainstream consumer product for all of these reasons. As a result, it struggles to fully realize its potential.

iPhone Duo is both an iPhone and a small iPad

iPhone Duo has the utility of an iPhone and a small iPad in a form factor that can fit in your pocket. It’s also the same price as say, buying an iPhone 16 Pro one year and upgrading to the iPhone 17 Pro the next year. That’s not unheard of.

Sure, iPhone Duo will have an uphill battle with software optimization, at least for third-party apps. But Apple has already crafted a highly considered story around the operating system and first-party apps. Developers will soon have the tools to make great apps for the versatile folding display as well.

The biggest challenge with the iPhone Duo, to me, is that it’s not the absolute best-in-class iPhone yet. Hopefully it can be in some future version.

	

It would be great to have the best of every iPhone in one device, including the foldable display. But for now, the iPhone 18 Pro still wins in the camera department and Face ID.

Importantly, those trade-offs won’t be missed for consumers curious to try a radically new iPhone form factor. 

In the kindest way possible, Apple Vision Pro wishes it had iPhone Duo’s challenges.

title: Google Search kicks off the NFL season with Live Game Feeds and fantasy football advice
snippet: Tonight’s game between the New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks isn’t just a Super Bowl LX rematch — it’s also the official start of the 2026 NFL season. Google has invested pretty heavily in football over the past few years through YouTube TV, but today, it’s giving Search some big improvements to make following the season a little easier. more…
fullText:
Tonight’s game between the New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks isn’t just a Super Bowl LX rematch — it’s also the official start of the 2026 NFL season. Google has invested pretty heavily in football over the past few years through YouTube TV, but today, it’s giving Search some big improvements to make following the season a little easier.

Google is adding a Live Game Feed to search, which allows fans and spectators alike to follow along with game developments as they unfold on the field. Any active game will show a “Live” icon in search, and selecting that option shows a recap of what’s happened so far alongside a “dynamic timeline featuring play-by-play updates, top social commentary, key video highlights, and AI-powered insights.” This sounds quite a bit like Google’s alternative to something like Apple’s (truly excellent) sports app, though we’ll have to see how it performs in action first.

Meanwhile, Search is also getting a new carousel display that shows other ongoing games whenever you search for a specific matchup, alongside a stats page that shows player-specific performance like rushing yards, sacks, and YAC, with favorability metrics on their way. Finally, Google has tuned AI Mode to assist with your fantasy football lineup, supporting Yahoo Fantasy and Sleeper account sync directly for real-time suggestions ahead of kickoff on Sunday.

Google’s new carousel view in Search is rolling out to all users globally on mobile. Live Game Feed is available in the US in English and currently supports NFL games, with a broader expansion and plans to add collegiate teams coming later this month. Fantasy football advice in AI Mode is, similarly, only available for English-language users in the US.

Any active game will show a “Live” icon in search, and selecting that option shows a recap of what’s happened so far alongside a “dynamic timeline featuring play-by-play updates, top social commentary, key video highlights, and AI-powered insights.” This sounds quite a bit like Google’s alternative to something like Apple’s (truly excellent) sports app, though we’ll have to see how it performs in action first.

title: The iPhone Duo is actually a software story

fullText:
Good morning, how did you sleep? Me, I had trouble until I started counting the number of times Apple used the word “AI” in its keynote (it was 41). In my dream, I was inundated with Elizabeth Holmes deepfakes and memes, which startled me awake. As I lay in bed, I calmed down by reading about how AI will “kill us all by the end of the decade,” and then I got up and helped ChatGPT do my kids’ homework. Such a great day.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column.

⭐️ Starred

Today’s main story is, of course, Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, which debuted two new iPhone 18 Pros, two new Apple Watches, an updated pair of AirPods at a lower price, and a foldable called the iPhone Duo.

	

As predicted (and pre-empted), the iPhone Duo is a book-style foldable slightly wider and shorter than the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. Apple uses a combination of flexible plastic and thin layers of titanium sandwiched between the OLED panel, and claims that the crease is basically undetectable, though we’ll have to see how well that claim holds up over time. Curiously, Apple has also resurrected the under-display camera, which was a mainstay of Samsung’s Fold line until it disappeared in the Fold 7, as well as Apple Pencil support, which Samsung also dropped in the same generation.

To the credit of Samsung, Oppo, Honor, and even Google, the iPhone Duo does not appear to be dramatically superior to the latest book-style foldables; it matches the latest Pixel Folds’ IP68 water and dust resistance rating (that degrades over time); it relies on a side-mounted fingerprint sensor for authentication over the more convenient Face ID; it only has two cameras, and they lack the upgraded features of the Pro models; and at 254 grams, it’s heavier than practically any other foldable out there today.

What I find more compelling than the hardware is how Apple designed iOS to ostensibly work better with a foldable. Watching the demos, you can immediately see the care that went into the transitions between main and internal displays, and the changes that make the software easier to use with one hand. And while older apps may look funky until they’re updated, Apple has traditionally had better luck than Google convincing (or forcing) developers to adapt their apps to new form factors.

With iOS 27.1, which will be released alongside the iPhone Duo in October, developers will be able to target the foldable in app updates. Apple is banking on the fact that this larger canvas will tempt developers with new ways to earn money, a flywheel that has rewarded the company handsomely over the past 18 years. And hopefully the new attention paid to Apple’s entry will push reluctant developers to consider doing the same for their Android apps — though I’m not holding my breath. 

More from 9to5Mac: Hands-on with the foldable iPhone Duo

✉️ Inbox

Hands-on: Honor’s Robot Phone is probably the coolest phone you still can’t buy. Straight from the IFA floor, Andrew goes hands-on with the most bizarre phone of 2026.

Xiaomi 18 Fold goes on sale with full specs and a Galaxy Z Fold 8 comparison. Xiaomi timed its iPhone Duo competitor perfectly or poorly depending on how you look at it. The phone is intriguing in its own right, with Xiaomi’s first home-grown SoC and a huge 200MP main camera.

Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max has a 13.3-inch display, Android 17, and a 12,000 mAh battery

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max melds a classic ARRI camera with an iPhone-like look, launches this month

Samsung’s Privacy Display and TriFold merge in the Huawei Mate XT2. Samsung may have abandoned the tri-fold category, so Huawei is just stealing its best ideas.

Oppo confirms Find X10 Pro Max and its triple 200MP camera setup will launch this month. Another big release for massive cameras, the Find X10 Pro Max follows the ridiculously well-endowed Find X9 Ultra, which our Ben Schoon called “simply stunning” in his review.

Two Galaxy S27 models will get Samsung’s Privacy Display, not just the Ultra. We’re still doing this, huh?

Hands-on: Orbitkey elevated its time-tested key organizer with a built-in Google Find Hub tracker. As someone who loses his keys all the time, this product just makes sense.

Pebblebee’s latest Android Find Hub trackers have bright neon colors, available today

Google Find Hub update brings new ‘Remembered’ tab with Gemini

Boox Picco is exceptionally tiny for an e-reader, but it parts ways with Android and third-party apps. I am an avowed fan of tiny e-readers, and I am also a Boox Palma 2 owner, so I’ll definitely be picking this up when it debuts in November.

Arm’s new CPU cores and GPUs for Android chips promise ‘desktop-class’ games, more AI power. This is the part where I joke about how excited I am to play a ray-traced version of Candy Crush or something, but Arm genuinely knocked it out of the park with this release.

Google Find Hub update brings new ‘Remembered’ tab with Gemini. I cannot wait to abuse the heck out of this feature.

Google Messages rolls out Keep Notes integration on Android. 

Google Search kicks off the NFL season with Live Game Feeds and fantasy football advice. Go Bills!

Today in bugs, bug fixes, and shutdowns:

Google Maps speedometer disappears on Android Auto for some, traffic data still missing too

Google Messages slowly rolling out fix for bug that randomly sends old texts to other people

Samsung is shutting down ‘Quick Measure’ and ‘AR Doodle’ apps for Galaxy phones

Google Pixel Tablet has been discontinued, out of stock everywhere

🍎 Etc.

Apple didn’t just introduce a foldable iPhone yesterday. There was also the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and the AirPods 5.

With the Duo stealing much of the spotlight, it may be easy to overlook the other products, but it’s worth sticking with them for a minute. The iPhones, for instance, feature an upgraded main sensor with a variable aperture, a spec that Samsung adopted with the Galaxy S9 and abandoned two years later. Apple’s implementation offers four stops of range (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0), which are cycled through automatically depending on the environment. I’m not sure how much real-world impact it will have, but the technology has likely come a long way in the past few years, so I’m cautiously optimistic.

Perhaps more interesting is that the iPhone 18 Pro is the first in Apple’s flagship lineup to do away with Qualcomm modems, a change seven years in the making. The C2, which is also in the Duo, is Apple’s first chip to support mmWave in the US, which is required for Verizon’s network. (Oddly, the iPhone 18 Pro Max retains its Qualcomm modem, perhaps because it performs better and can fit into the larger housing.)

The new Apple Watch’s most notable feature may be its most controversial: inside its overarching Audio Intelligence announcement are two features, Live Rewind and Siri Recap, that create transcriptions or summaries of recent interactions. While Apple is quick to point out that no audio data is uploaded to its servers, nor stored permanently on the watch, the reality is that this feature enables surreptitious recording of everyday conversations without consent.

The AirPods 5 is low-key interesting, not because of any particular upgrade but because it’s the only product in Apple’s entire lineup that received a price drop.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

Watch me and Will Sattelberg talk endlessly about the insane You Can See Everything trailer before dovetailing into a conversation about repairable tech with Fairphone CTO, Chandler Hatton. 

Afterwards, if you still have any brain cells left, you should watch this Metroid Ravenous trailer, which I’ve already seen half a dozen times, and then spend some time with Playdate Season 3, which drops in October.

🎙️ Quotations

I asked the 9to5Google editors to sum up their thoughts on yesterday’s Apple event.

This event really cemented Apple as just another player in the industry, if it wasn’t already. A Pro-tier iPhone leaning on AI tricks as the bulk of its pitch? A foldable that pulls from nearly a decade’s worth of other companies’ devices without bringing much new to the table? What was even new on the Watch Series 12 besides that awful new brown color? Whatever spark of creativity Apple once carried — even from an Android user’s perspective — has been long gone for a while now, but this is the first event where I really felt a burning sense of boredom in the pit of my stomach.

– Will Sattelberg, Senior Writer and Podcaster

The iPhone Duo was the highlight for me; Apple’s entrance to the foldable market was inevitable, and it was fairly well done.

I’m wary of things like the side-oriented UI changes to iOS and the glossy dot in the middle of a matte inner display, but Apple’s usual level of polish has me intrigued. Not enough to drop $2,000 on a device that runs an OS I absolutely loathe, though, especially seeing as Apple didn’t show off much that actually changes the game in terms of using a foldable. The most revolutionary addition was that neat animation when transitioning between displays. For now, I’m still loving my Fold 8.

– Ben Schoon, Senior Editor

Apple did in fact “just walk in” and possibly figure out foldables. That or the reality distortion field was upgraded.

Anyway, I’m personally interested in the Apple Pencil support for the iPhone Duo, while I’m very eager to see how the new sidebar that incorporates status bar icons and the dock feels on the Duo’s cover screen. Ignoring third-party launchers that you have to install yourself, this might be the biggest change in smartphone UX for a bit.

– Abner Li, Editor-in-Chief

No matter how you feel about the iPhone Duo as a device, it’s finally good to see competition begin to heat up for phones that function beyond the range of the smartphones we’ve been using for the over a decade. Unfortunately, that competition is also expensive, just like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Not entirely unexpected, but a nudging reminder of where technology’s economy is right now. I, for one, am excited to see how the iPhone Duo works in the same tests we throw Android foldables through. If the Duo UX looks as good as Apple’s pre-recorded event makes it out to be, there might be plenty to look forward to for both Apple and Android. And who knows, maybe the iPhone Duo 2 won’t be nearly $2,000.

– Andrew Romero, Senior Editor

After seeing the Duo in the hands of the public, it seems like Apple isn’t magically reinventing the foldable after all.

Apple’s take on foldable software is fun, with lots of good hardware choices that will hopefully positively influence Android foldables. But overall, it hasn’t addressed any huge problems that existing foldables aren’t already dealing with.

– Jordan Floyd, Video Producer

title: Report: iPhone Duo could give Apple a 25% share of foldable market in 2026
snippet: A new TrendForce report says the iPhone Duo is expected to capture 24,8% of the foldable smartphone market in 2026 alone, countering a 20% slump in the segment. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new TrendForce report says the iPhone Duo is expected to capture 24,8% of the foldable smartphone market in 2026 alone, countering a 20% slump in the segment. Here are the details.

iPhone Duo expected to ship 5 million units by the end of 2026

Following yesterday’s announcement of the iPhone Duo, TrendForce published a report today predicting that Apple will capture 24,8% of the foldable smartphone segment by the end of the year.

TrendForce expects Apple to ship 5 million units of the iPhone Duo in 2026, helping offset a segment-wide slowdown due to “sharp increases in component costs”:

TrendForce forecasts global foldable smartphone shipments of approximately 20.2 million units in 2026, up just 0.5% YoY. Excluding Apple, combined shipments from Android brands are expected to reach only around 15.2 million units, down more than 20% YoY.

The report notes that Samsung is still poised to lead the market with 7.1 million units shipped for the year and 35.1% market share, and expects Huawei to match Apple’s 5 million units shipped and 24.8% share.

TrendForce goes on to analyze some of Apple’s hardware choices for the iPhone Duo, including the trade-offs the company made to achieve its final design:

Apple has omitted a dedicated periscope telephoto camera to minimize thickness and conserve internal space. Instead, the 48 MP main camera provides 2x optical-quality zoom, while a side-mounted Touch ID sensor replaces Face ID. These choices highlight the trade-offs that foldable smartphones continue to face among device thickness, camera capabilities, biometric components, and battery space.

TrendForce rounds out the report by looking ahead at the foldable segment, suggesting that “deeper integration of AI and multitasking interfaces with the larger foldable display could transform the device from a hardware differentiator into a new interface for AI applications.”

title: This might be iPhone 18 Pro’s best camera feature for most users
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro packs lots of camera upgrades (great rundown here), with the tentpole addition being variable aperture. But there’s one other Main camera change that users like me might deem their favorite. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro packs lots of camera upgrades (great rundown here), with the tentpole addition being variable aperture. But there’s one other Main camera change that users like me might deem their favorite.

iPhone 18 Pro’s new f/1.48 lens could prove popular for the average non-‘pro’ user

As impressive as Apple’s new iPhone Duo foldable is, when it comes to camera features, it’s a clear loser to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max (see our iPhone Duo-iPhone 18 Pro comparison here).

Not only does iPhone Duo lack a Telephoto camera, but its Main camera also misses out on the improvements coming to iPhone 18 Pro.

For a rundown of iPhone 18 Pro camera upgrades, I recommend my colleague Ben’s piece here.

As I’ve been thinking about the new camera system, many of the changes appear meant for users that are more “pro” than me. All of the manual ‘Pro controls’ iPhone 18 Pro offers intimidate me, and I don’t expect to ever use them. Even the tentpole variable aperture feature feels a bit over my head, though I’m glad it can work automatically.

Relevant background: I have zero training in photography outside of a single ‘Today at Apple’ class I took years ago. But of course, I love to take photos with my iPhone.

And the iPhone 18 Pro camera change I’m most intrigued by is something highlighted by The Verge. Antonio G. Di Benedetto writes:

I think the real star feature of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera is its f/1.48 maximum aperture…People love bokeh. Last year’s Pro iPhone cameras had an f/1.7 aperture, and now being at f/1.48, the 18 Pro camera should work better in low-light as well as have a slightly shallower depth of field. Will f/1.48 be a huge difference in bokeh from f/1.7? Probably not. It’s likely to have depth of field that’s just a smidge shallower — but that’s the look that people often like.

I speak from experience here, as I usually shoot on full-frame cameras and one of my go-to lenses is a 50mm with an f/1.2 maximum aperture. A lens that fast, with depth of field that shallow gives a unique look that’s easy to overuse, but it almost never fails that people swoon when I take their portrait using that lens — with that blurry, “dreamy” blur isolating them from the background. The f/1.48 of the iPhone 18 Pro is obviously not going to compare to an f/1.2 on full-frame, but f/1.2 and similarly wide apertures on big sensors is the look that people often want to emulate. It’s the whole reason Portrait Modes on smartphones came into being in the first place.

I haven’t used an iPhone 18 Pro yet. But I wouldn’t be surprised if the new f/1.48 aperture proves a hit among users like me.

Most iPhone 18 Pro buyers will, I suspect, never touch any of the custom manual controls. But if their everyday photos offer more natural, “dreamy” bokeh—even if just a little bit—then the iPhone 18 Pro camera could be beloved for that reason alone.

Which iPhone 18 Pro camera features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

title: iOS 27.1 release date: Here’s when to expect the new iPhone update
snippet: iOS 27 launches for all users next week, and will be followed not long after by the first iOS 27.1 beta and public launch. Here’s when to expect iOS 27.1’s arrival. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 launches for all users next week, and will be followed not long after by the first iOS 27.1 beta and public launch. Here’s when to expect iOS 27.1’s arrival.

iOS 27.1 launches in October before iPhone Duo release, with beta in the next week or so

If you’re not running Apple’s beta already, there’s a huge iPhone software update coming next week.

iOS 27 launches this Monday, September 14 and is packed with new features like Siri AI.

But if you’ve been running the iOS 27 beta all summer, you’re likely already looking ahead to iOS 27.1.

Apple is expected to debut the first iOS 27.1 beta within about a week of iOS 27 launching. Here’s what we’ve seen in recent years:

iOS 26.1 beta released 7 days after iOS 26

iOS 17.1 beta released 9 days after iOS 17

iOS 16.1 beta released 2 days after iOS 16

I excluded iOS 18 because Apple launched its 18.1 beta extra early during the summer as a way to test Apple Intelligence.

So the typical pattern points to iOS 27.1 beta 1 arriving as early as next week, or as late as the week of September 21.

What about the public launch?

Apple confirmed this week that iOS 27.1 will ship by October 23—and likely a few days earlier.

Its iPhone Duo press release says, “iPhone Duo will be available with iOS 27.1.” Since iPhone Duo arrives in users’ hands on October 23, the software update must be released by then.

This will actually be slightly earlier than we’d normally expect. Starting with 2025, in the last four years Apple’s x.1 updates launched on: November 3, October 28, October 25, and October 24.

Based on iOS 27.1 shipping with iPhone Duo, the most likely public release date for the software is anywhere from Monday, October 19 to Wednesday, October 21.

It’s unknown what all will be included in the update other than iPhone Duo-exclusive changes. But we’ll keep you posted after the first beta arrives.

title: Google Maps speedometer disappears on Android Auto for some, traffic data still missing too
snippet: Android Auto users are reporting an issue where the Google Maps speedometer, available for mere months, is randomly vanishing. more…
fullText:
Android Auto users are reporting an issue where the Google Maps speedometer, available for mere months, is randomly vanishing.

Back in July, Google Maps on Android Auto finally started rolling out support for a live speedometer while navigating. This was alongside showing speed limits. It started more broadly rolling out later that month, but still hasn’t rolled out to everyone.

Now, in fact, we’re looking at the exact opposite happening. A number of users have reported on Reddit that the speedometer has suddenly vanished on Android Auto. It’s not a particularly widespread issue, it seems, but the rollout hasn’t expanded to all users in the first place. This is alongside traffic patterns, which are still missing for a number of users after breaking in late August. 

We’ve also noticed continued reports of Android Auto missing its signal indicator, an ongoing bug for months at this point.

	

Google rolls out new Android Auto updates on a pretty regular basis, along with Maps, but these isolated issues just don’t seem to be going away. Leave a comment below if you’re running into these problems.

title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: Here are Apple’s full release notes
snippet: Apple has announced that macOS 27 Golden Gate will ship to all users next Monday, September 14. Here are Apple’s official release notes for macOS 27. more…
fullText:
Apple has announced that macOS 27 Golden Gate will ship to all users next Monday, September 14. Here are Apple’s official release notes for macOS 27.

Apple’s official macOS 27 release notes now available

Today alongside shipping its RC (release candidate) updates, Apple published full release notes for iOS 27 and also for macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Here are the full, unedited macOS 27 release notes:

Experience the new Siri AI

Introducing Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by Apple Intelligence that’s more personal, more capable, and more conversational. It is integrated into Spotlight, so you can search for answers about almost any topic right from where you already search for things across your system. It can draw on personal context to find things across your messages, mail, photos, and more. And it can get things done across your apps, just by asking. Revisit and resume past conversations in the new dedicated Siri app, synced with iCloud across your Apple devices. Siri AI is rolling out to users, and you can get started by turning it on in Settings.

Take action on what’s onscreen

With Visual Intelligence, you can select a window of your screen and Siri can answer questions or take action with what’s onscreen, like adding events to your calendar. You can access Visual Intelligence with a dedicated keyboard shortcut — Command-Shift-Space.

Powerful new ways to edit photos

Use intelligent photo editing tools to reframe a photo after it’s been taken with Spatial Reframing or expand your shot with the Extend tool. And enhancements to Clean Up let you remove distractions with better quality and more realistic infill, even when the scene is complex.

New tools to browse in Safari

Automatically group your tabs into topics, so related pages are easier to find. With Notify Me, Safari can monitor pages for changes like price drops or restocks and alert you when it’s time to act. Describe an Extension lets you use natural language to create custom extensions, like adding a button to save your favorite recipes.

Easily create Shortcuts using natural language

With Describe a Shortcut, you can automate daily tasks with a simple description and all of the required steps are assembled on your behalf. For example, you can describe a shortcut to automatically text your partner when you’re headed home from work with an estimated arrival time based on traffic.

Even more refined design

Updates to Liquid Glass improve readability, and a new slider lets you customize how it looks, from ultra-clear to fully tinted. Uniform toolbars, edge-to-edge sidebars, and more detailed app icons further elevate the design.

New child safety features

Powerful new parental controls help parents more easily manage what content their children can see, who they can communicate with, and when they have access to apps. Ask to Browse requires kids to request permission before visiting any new website in Safari. Communication Safety expands its protections to help keep conversations safe. Time Allowances gives parents more flexible ways to manage the time kids spend in apps across categories, and offers guidance based on expert research that’s tailored to a child’s age. Schedules help manage which apps kids have access to at different times of the day and across the week.

A more responsive and delightful experience

An expansive set of improvements make your Mac even faster, more reliable, and easier to use. Better search in Spotlight and Mail helps you find what you’re looking for with greater ease. AirDrop Transfers and network file browsing happen faster. And many more improvements make your day-to-day use more enjoyable.

For information on the security content of Apple software updates, please visit: support.apple.com/100100.

Some features may not be available in all regions or on all Apple devices. To learn more, please visit: apple.com/macos/feature-availability.

Usage limits may apply for some Apple Intelligence features, including but not limited to Siri AI, Intelligent Photo Editing Tools, Image Playground and AFM 3 Cloud models in Shortcuts. To learn more please visit: apple.com/apple-intelligence.

Software updates, like this one, add new features and improvements that may affect performance and/or battery life. To learn more, please visit: support.apple.com/125039.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs Series 11: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 improves many of the core components that power watchOS and the device’s health and fitness features, plus unlocks new AI capabilities. Here’s everything new in Apple Watch Series 12 vs Series 11. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 improves many of the core components that power watchOS and the device’s health and fitness features, plus unlocks new AI capabilities. Here’s everything new in Apple Watch Series 12 vs Series 11.

Design and durability: New case options, Ceramic Shield 2, more

Apple Watch Series 12 comes in the same 42mm and 46mm options as before, but with some design and durability updates.

In terms of case options, Apple Watch Series 12 debuts a new Dark Bronze aluminum finish and also introduces Ceramic, which is available in Pearl White and Night Blue.

Aluminum models of Series 12 add Ceramic Shield 2 for tougher, more durable glass than what comparable Series 11 models had.

Additionally, there are minor size tweaks with the latest models:

42mm model is 37mm wide, up from Series 11’s 36mm

46mm model is 40mm wide, up from Series 11’s 39mm

The screen size remains the same, but the case being slightly larger results in bigger bezels.

Performance: New S11 chip, double the RAM

There’s a new, more powerful S11 chip in the Apple Watch Series 12, and it’s the first notable performance upgrade since 2023’s S9.

S11 enables new health and AI features that are exclusive to the latest models, as detailed below. Apple doesn’t say what impact it will have on other everyday tasks, but hopefully there’s a noticeable boost there too.

Apple Watch Series 12 also upgrades the memory of the Series 11, offering 4GB of RAM—double the 2GB from last year.

Health: New ‘Health Sensing System’ with key upgrades

With Apple Watch Series 12, Apple is introducing a new “Health Sensing System” that essentially represents an overhaul of the internal sensing components.

In real-world terms, here’s what’s changed and the benefits it brings per Apple:

Heart rate tracking: Second-generation electrical heart sensor and always-on optical heart sensor enable high-frequency background heart rate tracking that you can view on new Heart Rate watch face complication

HRV improvements: “now measured up to 24 times more often and available to view in a new section of the Heart Rate app”

New Recovery HRV: “best for identifying daily signals of stress and recovery”

Step tracking: More accurate, with new Steps complication to track steps in real time from watch face

Software: Audio Intelligence, new Readiness app, and more

It’s not often that new Apple Watch hardware comes with exclusive software features. But Apple has a variety of software-related updates that require Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4.

Audio Intelligence is what Apple calls a “brand-new class of Apple Intelligence features” powered by S11. Some features will be available at launch while others arrive in a software update in late 2026. New features include:

Siri Recap: “[creates] high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment.”

Live Rewind: “[helps] users recall what was just said in conversation. A double press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so users can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with.”

Shazam: “instantly detects the music playing around the user and automatically displays the song title and artist’s name on the Music Recognition widget in the Smart Stack”

Sound Recognition: “[alerts] users who are deaf or hard of hearing of important sounds, even when their iPhone isn’t with them. This feature listens for sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, or a baby crying, and uses on-device intelligence to notify users when they’re detected.”

Joining AI features is a new Readiness app powered by Series 12’s overhauled health sensors. Apple says:

Apple Watch Series 12 introduces readiness, a new feature that analyzes a user’s recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score to offer insight into their capacity for the day ahead. Readiness provides a single 0-10 score with a clear, actionable recommendation: Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. This helps a user decide how to take on their day, whether they’re headed into a workday or tackling their training plan.

As mentioned above, Series 12 also adds new watch face complications for tracking your steps and heart rate.

Battery: Faster charging, outdoor workout gains

Apple Watch Series 12 supports faster charging than Series 11, reducing the amount of time you have to go without wearing it. Per Apple:

Apple Watch Series 12: 15 minutes charge gets up to 12 hours battery life

Apple Watch Series 11: 15 minutes charge gets up to 8 hours battery life

Additionally, while overall quoted battery life is still 24 hours this year, you can now get up to 10 hours of battery during an outdoor workout. That’s 25 percent more than Series 11 supported.

Connectivity: GPS improvement

There’s one more small change: Apple’s website says that Series 12 features “Precision L1 GPS.” 

By contrast, Apple Watch Series 11 only features “GPS.” Adopting the L1 frequency band should enable Apple Watch Series 12 to deliver better GPS precision than before.

Apple Watch Series 12 is now available to pre-order at $399. It ships Friday, September 18.

title: The four-hour-long Elon Musk documentary might be preaching to the choir
snippet: It makes sense that Musk is a long film. The latest from Alex Gibney, who has previously directed documentaries about Theranos and Steve Jobs, is an impressively thorough retelling of the story of Elon Musk, from his early days as a dot-com millionaire to "taking a wood chipper" to vital US government departments. In order to understand Musk's rise to power, you need to know the whole story. Musk tells it compellingly and convincingly, but doesn't offer much in the way of revelations if you're aware of Musk's catastrophic influence on the world. For everyone else, a demanding runtime just shy of four hours might prove too much of a barrier t … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
It makes sense that Musk is a long film. The latest from Alex Gibney, who has previously directed documentaries about Theranos and Steve Jobs, is an impressively thorough retelling of the story of Elon Musk, from his early days as a dot-com millionaire to “taking a wood chipper” to vital US government departments. In order to understand Musk’s rise to power, you need to know the whole story. Musk tells it compellingly and convincingly, but doesn’t offer much in the way of revelations if you’re aware of Musk’s catastrophic influence on the world. For everyone else, a demanding runtime just shy of four hours might prove too much of a barrier to being convinced.

The film opens with shots of space and a voiceover of Musk detailing some of his sci-fi ambitions. From there, it’s a fairly chronological narrative of how we got to this point. The first section of the film reveals how Musk’s mythology was built, while also steadily seeding doubts that he’s the Tony Stark–style tycoon that many believe him to be. It starts off with the basic details, like when Musk was ousted as CEO from PayPal or how he convinced the world he founded Tesla, a company that existed before he was involved. The film juxtaposes his many bombastic claims about autonomous vehicles with visceral footage of a deadly crash involving a Tesla on autopilot. It drops in poignant interviews, like when former MAGA influencer Ashley St Clair, mother to one of Musk’s many children, declares in a terrified voice: “Elon is a nuke.”

At the outset, Gibney makes it clear that his goal is to answer two questions with interrelated answers: how Musk got so powerful, and why we allowed it to happen. By gradually accruing power through Tesla, X, SpaceX, and Starlink, Musk ingratiated himself with governments all over the world, in particular the US, and then used that political power to further his own interests once it became so hard to extricate his influence. The documentary lays out the plot clearly and concisely, all in one place.

Musk himself didn’t participate in the documentary. Instead, he sent Gibney a legal threat over it. So Gibney built in a digital doppelgänger that mouths to audio of things Musk actually said, based on a database the team created of existing clips. The avatar Musk veers into uncanny valley territory, with its overly expressive face and unsettling heavy breathing, but it’s a smart way of putting Musk’s face to his words, in a manner of speaking. And it fits well with Musk’s belief in simulation theory. Additionally, the movie uses plenty of sim and video game imagery to illustrate things throughout, like a fictional first-person shooter that depicts Musk dismantling Twitter and the US government with a chainsaw that shoots lasers. It’s over-the-top and absurd, but then again we’re here, in part, because of a kid bureaucrat named Big Balls.

In many ways, Musk is successful. It lays out how he got to power and why he was able to accrue so much of it without being stopped, which boils down to him being far too rich and ingrained by the time most people realized what was going on. Unfortunately, as someone who has followed the story over the years, I can’t say I learned much or gained new insights into the man while watching Musk.

Which makes me wonder who this film is for. Many people have already woken up to the fact that Musk is something quite different than some kind of genius inventor, but there are still plenty who only associate his name with past wins like incremental advances in reusable rockets or pre-Tesla Cybertruck vehicles. The film even interviews one fan who says he intentionally ignores the things about Musk that he doesn’t agree with. That’s exactly the kind of person who would benefit most from watching Musk lay it out all in one place.

But in a world of dwindling attention spans, four hours in a theater is a lot to ask (even if it does have a 10-minute intermission). It could miss the people who need to see it the most.

Musk is in theaters on October 16th. This review is based on a screening at the Toronto International Film Festival.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Shelly’s Flood S Gen4 is a low cost Matter leak sensor for Apple Home
snippet: Water damage is one of those problems where a single sensor can save you a major repair bill on your floors, cabinets, etc. Leak sensors have been among the best values in the smart home for years, and Shelly’s new Flood S Gen4 makes it even easier to get started. It’s under $30, Matter-certified, and works with Apple Home out of the box. more…
fullText:
Water damage is one of those problems where a single sensor can save you a major repair bill on your floors, cabinets, etc. Leak sensors have been among the best values in the smart home for years, and Shelly’s new Flood S Gen4 makes it even easier to get started. It’s under $30, Matter-certified, and works with Apple Home out of the box.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Bigger sensors

Most leak sensors on the market today use small metal pins on the bottom, which means water has to pool in exactly the right spot before anything triggers. Shelly went a different direction with its new sensor, with three large stainless steel pads spread across the bottom of the unit. A larger contact area means water is detected faster and in more places, which is the whole point of putting a sensor under a water heater or washing machine in the first place.

The pads are also sensitive enough to detect clean or low-conductivity water, such as AC condensate. These leaks are often a lot harder to detect. The Flood S Gen4 is also low profile enough to slide under appliances, behind toilets, and beneath sinks, which is exactly where you want these things to live.

Matter/Apple Home support

The Flood S Gen4 is Matter certified and supports Wi-Fi and Zigbee, so it works with Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, SmartThings, and Home Assistant. Once it’s in Apple Home, the automation possibilities open up:

Cut power to a washing machine or dishwasher the moment water is detected (if it’s on a smart outlet)

Trigger every smart bulb in your house

Simple alerts to your iPhone of a leak detected (incredibly helpful if out of town)

Modes, alarms, and battery life

There’s a built-in local alarm alongside the phone notification, so anyone actually in the house hears it even if their phone is in another room. Shelly includes two operating modes, flood detection and rain detection, plus three alarm profiles (intense, normal, and economic) that let you balance a leak detection speed against battery life. It runs up to two years on the included CR123A battery.

Wrap up

At under $30, this is the kind of accessory you buy 3-4 of without thinking. In front of the water heater, in front of the dishwasher, under the washing machine, and under the kitchen sink. Matter/Apple Home support lets you get alerts from the Home app and build your Apple Home automations around it. There’s a lot to like here, and nothing I don’t like. Trust me, a water sensor detector is the smartest investment you can buy for a smart home.

You can buy the Shelly Flood S Gen4 from Amazon or directly from Shelly.

On October 2, Apple TV will debut The Last First: Winter K2, a revealing documentary that “tells a complex, harrowing and moving story” of extreme mountain climbing, and currently holds a rare 100% Rotten Tomatoes score.

Focusing on a 2021 expedition, this documentary follows Icelander John Snorri Sigurjónsson and the Pakistani father-son team of Ali and Sajid Sadpara, a party of mountaineers who set out to be the first to summit K2 in the winter, when the mountain’s conditions are the cruelest. The men soon find themselves sharing the treacherous ascent with influencer climbers and their film crews, commercial expedition clients, and a Nepalese team no longer content to help Westerners achieve mountaineering glory. “The Last First: Winter K2” takes us to the icy heights and unpredictable weather of K2 and reveals a surprising and layered story — one of strategy and determination, class and caste, money and power — all under life-and-death circumstances.

title: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 needs battery banks that actually fit; iPhone Duo might help
snippet: Magnetic battery banks aren’t everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s hard to argue with the convenience factor they deliver. Samsung’s camera design already makes these difficult on Galaxy devices, but Galaxy Z Fold 8 only makes matters worse with a short form factor that leaves battery banks hanging way over the edge. iPhone Duo might help matters here, but the same old problem remains. more…
fullText:
Magnetic battery banks aren’t everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s hard to argue with the convenience factor they deliver. Samsung’s camera design already makes these difficult on Galaxy devices, but Galaxy Z Fold 8 only makes matters worse with a short form factor that leaves battery banks hanging way over the edge. iPhone Duo might help matters here, but the same old problem remains.

The Qi ring on Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is very low on any already-short frame, which leaves magnetic wallets and battery banks well out of place on the foldable, hanging down below the bottom of the device. It’s a problem begging for a solution, and one that other wide foldables are also going to run into.

Is the iPhone Duo the solution to Samsung’s problem?

Not just yet. The iPhone Duo is bringing about a new wave of smaller Qi2 battery banks to fit the short and stout form factor. BMX just launched one of the first models with a solid-state battery specifically designed to fit the Duo. It has a kickstand ring and a little display to show battery percentage, with 5,000 mAh of power and a fit that doesn’t hang below the bottom edge of Apple’s first foldable.

	

I was hoping this would work on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, but BMX tells 9to5Google that this power bank won’t fit on Samsung’s device due to the camera. Foiled again!

Samsung’s camera design continues to be a problem here, which is why it’s nice that Samsung might be moving to something new on some of its Galaxy S27 devices. But, in the meantime, it remains a problem for existing users.

While BMX says the battery bank won’t fit perfectly on the Fold 8, it’s likely still a major improvement. The $80 power bank is available for purchase now, and it probably won’t be the last battery designed for the Duo and, in turn, a better fit for the Fold 8.

fullText:
CNET has a series of pieces comparing the iPhone Duo to three current Android foldables. While it’s a little frustrating to tackle the comparisons separately, it seems clear that the site views Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 as the device the Duo needs to beat.

That’s in large part because the two devices share similar passport-style aspect ratios rather than the tall and thin design of other foldables, and are priced only $100 apart …

Dimensions

Samsung’s device is a little thinner both when folded and unfolded.

Folded

Unfolded

iPhone Duo

11.3mm

5.2mm

Fold 8

9.7mm

4.5mm

Dust-proofing

One major problem with early versions of Samsung’s foldables is their vulnerability to damage through trapped dust and dirt, and the Fold 8 still has this weakness. Its IP48 rating means that it’s fully waterproof, but only rated against protection from particles larger than a grain of sand. The iPhone Duo, in contrast, is rated as fully waterproof and dustproof.

Cameras

There’s really nothing in it when it comes to the main cameras. The Duo has 48MP main and ultrawide cameras, while those of the Fold 8 are 50MP. Neither device has a telephoto lens.

The Fold 8 has a 10MP selfie camera embedded on the outer display, while the Duo has a 12MP one. Samsung has put another 10 MP selfie camera on the inner display, and while Apple hasn’t revealed the specs on this, it seems to be a significantly lower resolution one based on video shooting supporting 1080p but not 4K.

Battery

As is usual, Apple doesn’t specify the battery capacity, so we’ll need to wait for teardowns to determine this. However, the company says that it will last for up to 24 hours in typical use. 

The Fold 8 offers faster wired charging, specifying 0% to 73% in 30 minutes, while Apple says the Duo gets to a 50% charge in the same time. However, Apple wins on wireless charging with full MagSafe support, while the Fold 8 lacks the magnets needed for Qi2 wireless charging.

9to5Mac’s Take

In practice, of course, most people want to remain within their existing ecosystem, be it Apple or Android. Comparisons across operating systems are only relevant when one or other device proves sufficiently appealing to entice people to switch.

My personal suspicion is that the iPhone Duo is better placed than most iPhones when it comes to tempting Android users attracted to the foldable form factor. Samsung’s poor track record with durability could prove critical when choosing such an expensive device – $1900 for the Fold 8 against $1999 for the Duo. Additionally, even Android fans seem to be widely admiring the beauty of Apple’s user interface.

title: Apple sets cutoff time for getting faster iPhone 18 Pro pre-order
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders start tomorrow, and you can “Get Ready” by making your selections in advance via the online Apple Store. Here’s the deadline for when those decisions need to be locked in ahead of pre-orders opening. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders start tomorrow, and you can “Get Ready” by making your selections in advance via the online Apple Store. Here’s the deadline for when those decisions need to be locked in ahead of pre-orders opening.

You can speed through iPhone 18 Pro pre-order line by making your selections in advance

This weekend, Apple launches pre-orders for iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

Typically pre-orders start the Friday after an iPhone unveiling. But this year, likely due to today being 9/11, Apple pushed pre-orders back a day.

iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders begin Saturday, September 12 at 8:00 a.m. ET / 5:00 a.m. PT.

If you want to ensure the fastest possible pre-order, Apple lets you ‘Get Ready’ in advance.

Inside the Apple Store app or on Apple’s website, you can choose the ‘Get Ready’ button to make your iPhone selections ahead of the official pre-order time.

By doing this, you’ll speed up the process of completing the pre-order Saturday morning.

But there’s a cutoff time for this quicker pre-order option. Per Apple:

Customers have until 9 [p.m.] PT on Friday, September 11, to bypass the morning rush by selecting their model, pairing accessories, securing leasing or financing pre-approval, and setting up their trade-in.

Currently Apple’s press release actually says “9 a.m. PT” instead of “p.m.,” but that appears to be an error. Last year the cutoff time was 9 p.m., and currently it’s already past 9 a.m. PT and the ‘Get Ready’ option is still available. Additionally, the press release didn’t even go live until 9 a.m. PT, another sign that it should say “p.m.” instead.

So if you want to ensure your iPhone 18 Pro pre-order process goes as quickly and smoothly as possible, make your selections before 9:00 p.m. PT tonight.

title: Here’s why I left T-Mobile for an MVNO
snippet: I had been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when the company introduced its T-Mobile ONE plan. I had a military discount the entire time I was with them, but even with that discount my bill eventually ballooned to $113 a month thanks to T-Mobile’s price hikes. I decided enough was enough, so I started looking for a cheaper alternative. Plus, with Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro costing at least $100 more this year, I thought cutting my cell phone bill might help soften the blow if I upgraded to a new device. And so, I sought out an MVNO. more…
fullText:
I had been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when the company introduced its T-Mobile ONE plan. I had a military discount the entire time I was with them, but even with that discount my bill eventually ballooned to $113 a month thanks to T-Mobile’s price hikes. I decided enough was enough, so I started looking for a cheaper alternative. Plus, with Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro costing at least $100 more this year, I thought cutting my cell phone bill might help soften the blow if I upgraded to a new device. And so, I sought out an MVNO.

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for “Mobile Virtual Network Operator.” In simple terms, an MVNO is a wireless carrier that doesn’t operate its own nationwide cellular network. Instead, it purchases access to an existing network from one of the major carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon) and sells that service to its own customers. Think of them as wireless middlemen.

This means that switching to an MVNO doesn’t necessarily mean giving up the network you’re already using. For example, Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile’s network, Visible uses Verizon’s, and US Mobile gives customers the option of using networks from all three major carriers. For the purposes of this article, I’ll be focusing on these three MVNOs because they’re the ones I looked at most closely before leaving T-Mobile, but there are several other options out there as well.

Put simply, an MVNO gives you another way to buy cellular service without necessarily buying it directly from the company that owns the network.

Why are MVNOs cheaper and what’s the “catch?”

If an MVNO can use the same cellular networks as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how it can charge so much less? The simple answer is that MVNOs don’t have to shoulder all of the costs associated with operating a nationwide wireless carrier. They don’t have to build and maintain their own networks, many operate primarily online rather than maintaining physical retail locations, and they tend to have fewer employees. These savings can be passed along to customers in the form of lower monthly prices.

MVNOs also tend to offer simpler plans without many of the “perks” and extras that have become common with traditional wireless carriers. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get free streaming services or other incentives designed to keep you with a major carrier. But the money you save with an MVNO could easily offset the cost of those “free” perks if you actually want them.

That was certainly the case for me. I always looked forward to the free MLB.TV subscription included with T-Mobile and used it every season, but I never watched Netflix, so the “Netflix on Us” perk was wasted on me. Even if I wanted Netflix and MLB.TV, however, I could simply pay for them myself and still come out ahead with the money I saved by switching. At the end of the day, I mostly just wanted a reliable and more affordable cellular service, and I didn’t need T-Mobile to throw in a bunch of extras to get one.

The “catch” isn’t necessarily that the service is worse. It’s that you’re paying for fewer things. And exactly what you give up depends on the MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming may be limited to lower resolutions, the amount of high-speed or premium data you get may vary, and network priority can also differ. At home, I have very fast Wi-Fi and rarely find myself in “congested” areas like concerts or stadiums, so network priority was much less of a concern for me in normal, day-to-day use. But I do occasionally travel overseas, so international data was an important factor. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others require an additional fee or offer more limited coverage when you travel outside the U.S.

Then there are some less obvious differences, particularly when it comes to buying a new iPhone. Apple Card Monthly Installments and the iPhone Upgrade Program aren’t available when you choose an MVNO as your carrier. If you want to use either of those options, you’re limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. In practice, that means you’ll generally need to buy your iPhone outright if you’re purchasing it directly from Apple. The major carriers can also offer large trade-in credits and other promotions that aren’t generally available through MVNOs. Apple Watch support isn’t universal either, so that’s something to check if you have a cellular Apple Watch.

Finally, most MVNOs rely more on phone and chat support than physical stores with face-to-face employees. I consider myself tech-savvy, and I have no desire to wait in line in a store for help. And in my experience, some sales rep in the store is just going to call and get put on hold with the same people I’d end up calling from home anyway so this was not a dealbreaker for me.

The important thing is that none of these are universal limitations of MVNOs. They vary by carrier and plan, which means it’s worth looking at what you’re actually getting before you make the switch.

Three MVNOs worth considering

Once I’d made up my mind to leave T-Mobile, I started looking at alternatives. Postpaid plans on Verizon and AT&T were more expensive than what I was already paying, so both the other two big carriers were a no-go for me. I ultimately narrowed my search down to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each appealed to me for a different reason, and all three offered a way to significantly lower my monthly wireless bill without giving up access to a major carrier’s network.

US Mobile is perhaps the most flexible of the three, and the carrier I ultimately chose when switching from T-Mobile. That doesn’t mean it’s necessarily the best fit for you, or even the best MVNO of the three. It simply happened to be the best fit for me.

In fact, US Mobile wasn’t my first choice. I hadn’t even heard of the company before I started researching MVNOs. But the more I looked at what it offered, the more it stood out. Here’s why: US Mobile offers service on all three major U.S. networks, allowing customers to choose the network that works best for them. It also offers a Multi-Network add-on that allows you to have two networks active on the same iPhone (your add-on line remains active in the background), and your iPhone can switch to the second network if coverage is unavailable or weaker on your primary network (“when coverage is low,” according to US Mobile). “Allow Cellular Data Switching” must be enabled under your iPhone’s “Cellular Data” settings in order to take advantage. US Mobile does charge extra for this feature, and it’s not one I need, but it’s a neat one to have on offer.

I recently moved and was curious how Verizon’s coverage compared with T-Mobile’s near my new home, so I decided to test both networks. I set my wife’s iPhone up on US Mobile’s Light Speed network (which uses T-Mobile) and my iPhone on Warp (which uses Verizon) so we could compare the coverage for ourselves. As it turned out, Verizon was noticeably better in our area, so switching to US Mobile ended up being a win-win: better coverage and significantly less expensive service.

Mint Mobile was my first choice initially because T-Mobile owns it, meaning I could keep using the same network I was already familiar with while paying considerably less for it. What I didn’t like was the lack of included international data. My wife and I like to cruise, and with international travel being a regular part of our lives, having cellular data outside the U.S. is important to us. Mint offers international data, but it comes at an additional cost, which can quickly eat into some of the savings. I also didn’t like that taxes and fees cost extra.

Visible is similarly straightforward, but it runs exclusively on Verizon’s network. My biggest hesitation with Visible was Verizon’s coverage in my area. I had been a T-Mobile customer for nearly a decade, so I knew exactly what to expect from T-Mobile’s network, but I had no idea how Verizon’s coverage would compare. That was really the only thing holding me back from choosing Visible over US Mobile, which gave me the option to try Verizon’s network while still having access to T-Mobile and AT&T if Verizon didn’t work out. Visible also offers a free cellular Apple Watch plan with its highest-tier unlimited plan, which was another appealing feature. (US Mobile offers the same benefit on its highest-tier plan when using Warp, its Verizon network.)

What you’ll need to switch

Switching to an MVNO was easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones and transferred both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile in about ten minutes. I didn’t even have to leave the couch. You’ll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, but I am focusing on iPhone) and some information from your current carrier. And if you want to keep your existing phone number, make sure you don’t cancel your old service before the number has been transferred.

Here’s what you’ll need in order to switch:

The account number for your current wireless carrier

A transfer PIN

An unlocked, compatible iPhone

A new eSIM

A little patience

I paid the upfront annual price for two unlimited plans on US Mobile in preparation for the switch. My wife doesn’t have a cellular Apple Watch and doesn’t care about higher-quality video, so she opted for US Mobile’s Unlimited Starter plan, saving $100 compared with the Unlimited Premium plan that I chose. Paying $500 for two lines with an Apple Watch plan for a year seemed like a great deal compared with the $1,356 per year I was paying T-Mobile for two lines and no Apple Watch service. (And again, just to emphasize, that was with a military discount!)

Generating a transfer PIN through T-Mobile was a straightforward process, which I half-expected to be more buried and complicated than it actually was. Here are the instructions for Verizon and AT&T as well.

With my iPhone connected to Wi-Fi, US Mobile emailed me a new eSIM, and installing it was as simple as tapping a button in the email and following the onscreen instructions. It was the same process for my wife’s iPhone. The only additional step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I was able to do easily through US Mobile’s app.

Why I’m sticking with an MVNO

Same coverage for less money: For the money I’m saving, the concessions I’ve made are more than worth it. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, so cellular data simply isn’t as important to me (though in speed tests, US Mobile’s speeds are just as fast as T-Mobile’s were). What matters most is having a strong, reliable cellular signal when I’m away from Wi-Fi, particularly for making and receiving calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have done away with traditional contract plans, instead shifting to device payment plans that effectively serve the same purpose by keeping you tied to their network until you pay off your phone. I always buy my iPhone directly from Apple because I want the freedom that comes with an unlocked model, but I like that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible don’t require contracts.

Easy to switch: Most MVNOs let you pay month to month, so you aren’t locked into a long-term commitment. If one carrier has a deal one month and another carrier has a better deal the next, it’s quick and easy to switch. There’s also no credit check with prepaid accounts, which means your credit won’t take a hit every time a carrier makes an inquiry, unlike with postpaid accounts, and you can’t be denied because of your credit history. My credit is good, but I still don’t want it to take a hit if I decide to switch from T-Mobile to Verizon and they do a hard inquiry.

	

More savings if you pay annually: The trade-off for that flexibility is that you’ll save more if you’re willing to pay for a year of service upfront. Most MVNOs offer a significant discount for annual plans, so you’re giving up some of the freedom to switch whenever you want in exchange for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I like to cruise. If you’ve ever forgotten to put your iPhone into Airplane Mode on a ship and it connected to the ship’s cellular network, you’re in for a rude awakening and potentially a massive bill. With a prepaid plan, I don’t have to worry about accidentally racking up a massive roaming bill. If international roaming isn’t included, my phone simply won’t connect to an overseas network and charge me for it. Taxes and fees are also included in US Mobile’s plans, so the price listed is the price you’ll actually pay.

Switching to an MVNO wasn’t just about finding the cheapest service I could, but about getting the service I wanted without paying for a bunch of things I didn’t want or need. And so far, I haven’t felt like I’m missing out on anything that matters to me (though I know I will definitely miss the free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I even gained an Apple Watch line that I didn’t have before while still paying less. I have the same iPhones, the same phone numbers, my coverage is actually better in my area on US Mobile’s Warp (Verizon) network, and I have the freedom to switch again if I find a better option down the road.

Your priorities may be different from mine, and an MVNO won’t necessarily be the right choice for everyone. But if you’re paying a lot for your wireless service and haven’t considered an MVNO, it’s worth taking a look. You might be surprised by how little you actually give up.

title: ‘Lenovo Googlebook 15’ specs leak in full with ‘Google facial authentication’
snippet: Following some past leaks, another new report reveals basically everything about the upcoming “Lenovo Googlebook 15” including its full specs, but without a price tag. more…
fullText:
Following some past leaks, another new report reveals basically everything about the upcoming “Lenovo Googlebook 15” including its full specs, but without a price tag.

Google said that the first wave of Googlebook laptops would have a premium focus, and the company wasn’t kidding based on this latest leak. MacObserver has a full spec sheet for the “Lenovo Googlebook 15” and, between the OLED display an up to 32GB of RAM, this thing is not going to be cheap by any means.

Here are the highlights:

Intel Core Ultra 5 325

16GB / 32GB LPDDR5x RAM

256GB / 512GB storage

15.3-inch, 2880 x 1800 OLED, 120hz, 16:10, touchscreen

70Wh battery, up to 11 hours

Haptic trackpad (150x95mm)

2x USB-C/Thunderbolt 4, USB-A, HDMI 2.0, audio jack

Fingerprint sensor & “Google facial authentication”

A few things worth noting here.

	

To reiterate, this laptop will not be cheap. The closest comparison I could find was the ThinkPad X9 15 Aura Edition which Lenovo sells for just over $1,500 at the moment. It’s not like it doesn’t have the specs or features to back up that price – haptic trackpad and a fingerprint sensor are both great add-ons here – but will Googlebook’s software be able to make that worthwhile?

The most interesting tidbit here is mention of “Google facial authentication.”

There’s no added explanation in the report, but this is presumably referring to camera-based face unlock that was rumored to show up on Chromebooks and Pixel phones. “Project Toscana” is supposedly in the same ballpark as Apple’s Face ID in terms of speed, but details are still fuzzy on what this might end up being, and it’s unclear if these alleged hardware-based enhancements are actually in place on this laptop – it could be a simple software implementation, similar to Pixel phones.

We’ll likely be hearing more about Lenovo’s Googlebook and models from several other brands in the near future.

title: Samsung Galaxy SmartTag 3 copies the worst part of Apple’s AirTag in leak
snippet: Trackers like Apple’s AirTag have been a great piece of added utility to the mobile ecosystem, and every option has a slightly different look and feel. Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is rumored to be launching soon and, thanks to a pair of leaks, we know exactly what to expect. more…
fullText:
Trackers like Apple’s AirTag have been a great piece of added utility to the mobile ecosystem, and every option has a slightly different look and feel. Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is rumored to be launching soon and, thanks to a pair of leaks, we know exactly what to expect.

SammyGuru and Dealabs have both obtained more details on the upcoming Galaxy SmartTag 3, starting with some official-looking images from the former.

These reveal that Samsung’s new design lacks any sort of built-in mounting mechanism. Instead, the squircle shape requires an add-on to be connected to a keychain, bag loop, or anything else. It does result in a smaller design from the looks of it, but it’s a pretty big departure.

As pictured below, both prior generations of Galaxy SmartTag have had some sort of built-in loop for mounting, and this is also commonplace among other third-party smarttrackers from the likes of Pebblebee, Chipolo, and more. Apple’s AirTag, Motorola’s Moto Tag, and Google’s upcoming Pixel Tag all lack built-in mounting options too, though.

	

Functionally, this leak also reveals that SmartTag 3 will have UWB and Bluetooth, as well as an IP67 rating and around 500 days of battery life. There’s no mention of what network it will use, but it’s almost certainly exclusive to Samsung’s network rather than using Google’s Find Hub network in any capacity.

The other report claims pricing will be unchanged at €39.99 ($29.99 US), though a 4-pack will go from €129.99 to $139.99 this time around.

A release date is unclear, but Samsung certainly has plenty of other announcements in the pipeline.

title: Google upgrades all Gemini side panels in Workspace to have the same features
snippet: Gemini in Google Workspace can now “complete complex, cross-app tasks” from whatever app you’re working in. more…
fullText:
Gemini in Google Workspace can now “complete complex, cross-app tasks” from whatever app you’re working in.

Previously, the Gemini side panels found in each Workspace app had capabilities specific to that service: “generating a personalized document with Gemini required being in Docs while building AI-powered spreadsheets required being in Sheets.”

Google is now upgrading each instance of Gemini in Workspace to have the same feature set. This applies to the side panels in Gmail, Drive, Docs, Slides, and Chat. The upgrade is made possible by Workspace Intelligence and deeper app integrations.

For example, you can have Gemini “send an email to my sales team for their review and feedback” from Google Docs instead of needing to be in Gmail. 

	

In Google Chat, you can “find open times, schedule meetings, or resolve calendar conflicts.” Google Tasks also lets you “instantly log a reminder or create a to-do list” from any service.

On the content creation front, example prompts include:

When in Gmail (via the side panel) to create a doc: “Create a strategy brief for this project with goals, milestones and next steps.“

When in Gmail (via the side panel) to create a spreadsheet: “Create a tracker for this project in a new spreadsheet”

When in Docs (via the side panel) to create a deck: “Turn this proposal into an easy to read slide deck for my director using @presentation as a style reference.”

When in Chat (via Ask Gemini in Chat) to create a document: “Create a deck outlining Project Zebra with the latest updates”

When in Drive (via Ask Gemini in Drive) to create a document: “Create a customer insights deck from project Zebra using my project files including sheets, reports, and emails”

This expanded feature set started rolling out this month. For consumers, this is available to subscribers of Google AI Pro (“with the exception of scheduling functionality”) and Google AI Ultra. It’s also coming to:

Business: Standard and Plus

Enterprise: Standard and Plus

Other Editions: Frontline Plus (only for scheduling functionality)

Education Add-ons: Google AI Pro for Education

Other Add-ons: AI Expanded Access

title: Possible Google device at FCC could be Wear OS-powered fitness tracker
snippet: A new piece of hardware passed through FCC certification today, and the evidence points to it being a Wear OS-powered device made by Google. more…
fullText:
A new piece of hardware passed through FCC certification today, and the evidence points to it being a Wear OS-powered device made by Google.

This “Wireless Device” — as it’s officially labeled — comes from Goertek, which is already known for manufacturing various generations of Pixel Buds.

The “G8BL6” model name matches Google’s usual pattern for first-party hardware. Meanwhile, the e-label points to the existence of a screen, with the access method being Settings > System > Regulatory Information. That is identical to how you access the e-label on the Pixel Watch today. 

This would suggest the presence of Wear OS, with that possibility further bolstered by how the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) was leveraged during the testing process.

	

On the connectivity front, this device has Bluetooth LE and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), or GPS. The former uses a “Metal frame Antenna.”

Taken together, G8BL6 is most likely a Google fitness tracker powered by Wear OS, though the lack of Wi-Fi is curious. This would be a new form factor for the platform, raising questions about whether the OS is battery-efficient enough.

This filing comes as an unknown Google tracker was spotted in Pixel 11 advertising this August. We saw a vertical, pill-shaped display with a Pixel Watch-esque band. The watch face is very familiar, down to the existing Wear OS complications for fitness.

Following the Fitbit Air, this would make sense as a successor to the popular Fitbit Charge line, which is currently priced at $160 and last updated in 2023.
