title: The Duo is drool-worthy, but the iPhone 18 Pro camera features win for me
snippet: If ever there was a head versus heart moment in terms of Apple tech, it was in yesterday’s unveiling of the new iPhones. I already started the morning by wiping the drool from my desk after watching the iPhone Duo sections of yesterday’s keynote, but the true hero of yesterday’s show for me was the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, thanks to the new camera features … more…
fullText:
If ever there was a head versus heart moment in terms of Apple tech, it was in yesterday’s unveiling of the new iPhones.

I already started the morning by wiping the drool from my desk after watching the iPhone Duo sections of yesterday’s keynote, but the true hero of yesterday’s show for me was the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, thanks to the new camera features … 

The variable aperture – with caveat

Given the supply chain needed to introduce a variable aperture lens to the iPhone, it was no surprise that this was well and truly leaked prior to the launch. The only thing that wasn’t completely clear is whether the feature would be included in both iPhone Pro models or just the Pro Max, and the good news is that the former applies.

Apple also confirmed that while the iPhone will vary the aperture automatically in some cases, we can also take full manual control. I said beforehand that we might need to temper our expectations of just how much difference the feature will make.

The main limiting factor of iPhones is not the lens aperture – which is already rather wide – but rather the size of the sensor. Again, all else being equal, the larger the sensor, the shallower DOF you’ll be able to achieve. Compared to DSLRs and mirrorless cameras, iPhones have absolutely tiny sensors, and that isn’t going to change this year. Given the same size sensor and a very slightly wider aperture, physics would suggest that we shouldn’t expect very much.

But I also speculated about whether Apple might have improved the Portrait mode capabilities in this latest model and actually be using a combination of the wider aperture and computational photography in order to deliver a more impressive result than would be obtained from the hardware alone. That remains to be seen, but based on some of the sample photos shown, I do suspect I may have been right about this.

I’ll be experimenting with this and will of course share the results.

Low-light photography and videography

The widest aperture is also close to one stop brighter – up from f/1.78 in the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48. While it may not make much difference to depth of field in itself, it should be a worthwhile improvement for low-light captures, including night shots.

Manual control of shutter speed

In addition to being able to manually control the aperture, we can also select the shutter speed for both still photos and video.

For still photos, that means the ability to take long exposure photos. The promotional video demonstrated using this to achieve motion blur. We don’t yet know the maximum exposure time possible, and whether a combination of the narrowest aperture and computational trickery will allow 30-second exposures, which are commonly used to make flowing water look silky smooth. The same technique can also be used to remove passers-by from a scene.

With conventional cameras, that requires a neutral density filter to cut down the amount of light, but there are third-party iPhone apps that can combine a whole series of photos into a single image to achieve a similar effect. I quite frequently use the Spectre app in this way.

For video, manual control of the shutter speed allows us to use the 180-degree rule. When shooting at 24 frames per second, we want the shutter speed set to 1/48th of a second to achieve the most natural-looking motion blur. This is something we can do in third-party pro camera apps like Blackmagic Cam, but it’s great to have the same capability in the stock Apple one.

White balance control

Another feature found in third-party apps is white balance control, and this too now comes to the stock app.

For still photography, this allows us to adjust the color temperature to our taste, but it’s most important in video footage. Automatic white balance means that the color temperature, and thus the whole look of the scene, can change during a clip. This creates a very visibly amateurish look. Being able to lock white balance for the duration of a clip is a huge improvement.

Cinematic mode for all video footage

Cinematic mode is the video equivalent of Portrait mode, allowing us to apply an artificial shallow depth of field effect. So far, we’ve always had to choose between shooting standard video and Cinematic mode footage – though the latter does actually give us a flat file also. The iPhone 18 Pro lets us decide afterwards to apply Cinematic mode effects to standard video footage.

Additionally, we can now shoot Cinematic video at up to 60 frames per second, allowing it to be used for slow motion footage. 

Smart focus mode for video

Existing iPhones already allow us to set the focus to track a particular person within a scene, but the iPhone 18 Pro introduces a significantly more advanced version of this.

In particular, it appears to use AI to identify a particular individual so that it can continue reliably tracking them even when somebody else passes between us and our subject. Additionally, it will re-lock on them if they leave the frame and re-enter it while shooting.

Histogram

This feature was reported ahead of yesterday’s keynote, so I’ll simply echo what I said then.

Judging exposure visually can be extremely unreliable, especially when viewing the iPhone screen in bright sunlight. Most dedicated cameras support a histogram feature intended to provide an accurate depiction of the exposure.

Battery life

Shooting video can burn through battery life, so an improvement here is welcome. We don’t know the specifics for this use, but since the maximum life of the Pro Max is up from 39 hours to 45 hours, that suggests we should expect to get around 15% more shooting time over last year’s model.

Apple Reference Image

Finally, there is a way to prove the authenticity of a photo should that be required. This is obviously a specialist tool most relevant to roles like photojournalism and law enforcement.

Wrap-up

Sure, some people are going to have eyes only for the iPhone Duo, and that’s perfectly understandable. But if your iPhone is an important part of your camera lineup, then the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are the champions here.

title: Today’s NYT Strands Hints, Answers and Help for Sept. 13, #924
snippet: Here are hints and the answers for today’s NYT Strands puzzle, No. 924 for Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026.
fullText:
Looking for the most recent NYT Strands puzzle answers? CNET publishes daily answers and hints for The New York Times Mini Crossword, Connections, Connections: Sports Edition and Strands puzzles.

Strands is like a word find game, but without the list of words to find. Sometimes I see the theme and begin recognizing the answers right away. But for those times when I can’t seem to manage this, there’s a loophole: Strands lets you make as many words of four or more letters as you want. For every three of those words you find, the puzzle will highlight one of the answers. You’re still going to have to unscramble that answer, though, which can be very tough.

I go into depth about the rules for Strands in this story. 

James Bond fans, this puzzle might be one for you. You’ll recognize the theme as the words start to fill in. Read on for hints and all the answers.

Hint for today’s Strands puzzle

Today’s Strands theme is: Top secret.

If that doesn’t help you, here’s a clue: 007.

Clue words to unlock in-game hints

Your goal is to find hidden words that fit the puzzle’s theme. If you’re stuck, find any words you can. Every time you find three words of four letters or more, Strands will reveal one of the theme words. These are the words I used to get those hints, but any words of four or more letters that you find will work:

COUNT, COUNTER, PURE, GREY, TANG, GNAT, RATE, SOLE, RATER, STEER, CRED, CREDIT, RECOUNT

These are the answers that tie into the theme. The goal of the puzzle is to find them all, including the “spangram,” a theme word that reaches from one side of the puzzle to the other. When you have all of them (I originally thought there were always eight, but learned that the number can vary), every letter on the board will be used. Here are the nonspangram answers:

MOLE, AGENT, ASSET, PLANT, OPERATIVE, COUNTERSPY

Today’s Strands spangram

NYT/Screenshot by CNET

Today’s Strands spangram is UNDERCOVER. To find it, start with the U that’s four letters down on the far-left row, and wind down and then across.

Toughest Strands puzzles

Here are some of the Strands topics I’ve found to be the toughest.

#1: Dated slang. Maybe you didn’t even use this lingo when it was cool. Toughest word: PHAT.

#2: Thar she blows! I guess marine biologists might ace this one. Toughest word: BALEEN or RIGHT. 

#3: Off the hook. Again, it helps to know a lot about sea creatures. Sorry, Charlie. Toughest word: BIGEYE or SKIPJACK.

title: BlizzCon 2026: New Starcraft Shooter, Diablo 5, World of Warcraft Forever
snippet: News and trailers from Blizzard’s opening ceremony.
fullText:
In a packed, rowdy BlizzCon main hall, the game developer finally confirmed the rumors: We’re getting a shooter set in the Starcraft universe. The game is titled simply Starcraft.

All we saw was a brief teaser that showed the rise and sudden fall of an elite soldier. Still, Starcraft (the game) is the first major news from Starcraft (the series) in a decade, when Starcraft 2’s Nova Covert Ops campaign pack was released. The announcement of the franchise’s return rocked the enormous main hall at BlizzCon. 

I grew up playing the original Starcraft, spending late nights in custom games with friends, so I’m interested to see whether (and how) Blizzard can revitalize the franchise.

The game is planned for a 2030 launch, a full two decades after the release of StarCraft 2.

Diablo 5 announced, alongside Netflix series

In 2029, Sanctuary will finally fall. Players will fight to take it back in Diablo 5. 

In a dark and hazy main hall, Blizzard Entertainment showed a short teaser revealing Diablo’s return at the BlizzCon opening ceremony. For the series’ 30th anniversary, Diablo announced plans to drag players deeper into the darkness than they’ve ever seen. Diablo 5 will show us what happens when the Lord of Terror finally takes over the world. 

According to Diablo devs, the game will explore the question of what you must become to save a world that has already fallen. 

The past two Diablo games spent about a decade in development, so the announcement of the next entry is earlier than expected. We just wrapped the Mephisto storyline, and here comes Diablo announcing his (eventual) return. 

In the meantime, there’s still more planned for Diablo 4, which released its Lord of Hatred expansion earlier this spring. Blizzard will add the Amazon class — a returning favorite from Diablo 2 — via a class pack next year. It’s not a full expansion, but it gives players the opportunity to explore the Skovos Isles, home of the Amazons, as one of their own.

Blizzard CEO Johanna Faries also announced that an animated Diablo series is coming to Netflix and hinted that there may be more planned for other franchises sometime in the future.

World of Warcraft is forever, and Forever comes in November

The rumored “Classic plus” is coming to Blizzard’s flagship MMO. Titled World of Warcraft Forever, the game will funnel new content to players while preserving the feel (and level cap) of vanilla WoW.  

WoW Forever will add three new zones, overhaul several existing zones, drop 1,000 new quests into the game alongside nine new dungeons, two new raids and a new Skyborne race. 

Perhaps most surprisingly, the beta for WoW Forever opens on Thursday, and the game is set for a launch in less than two months, on Nov. 4.

Over in contemporary WoW, the latest expansion, Midnight, is entering the next phase of its story. Blizzard showed us a new cinematic that raised the stakes in ways that, as a non-WoW player, I frankly didn’t really follow, but it looked momentous. 

We also got a tease for the next expansion, The Last Titan, which will conclude the Worldsoul trilogy of expansions that began with 2024’s The War Within. 

Alongside a 3.0 update to Warcraft 3: Reforged, a remaster of the classic real-time strategy game, Blizzard is releasing a new Forsaken Kingdom campaign, launching today.

Overwatch finally reworked Roadhog and Sombra (again)

Blizzard’s hero shooter had its big moment earlier this year, when the game announced 10 new heroes for its 10th anniversary, plus a new, ongoing story that has spanned everything from cinematics to in-game map changes. The game’s BlizzCon announcements weren’t as big as those of other franchises, but there were still some surprises tucked away.

We got our first look at Doctrine, a vampire-inspired support hero who will join the roster in season 5 next month. Doctrine is playable this weekend in a hero preview before joining the roster permanently in October.

The game is also adding a new escort map, set in the Icelandic prison that contained Doctrine before Doomfist and his crew of ex-Talon members broke him out. 

A new support hero and a new map were expected. What really made me shoot forward in my seat was the announcement that hero reworks are starting to come through — and longtime damage hero Sombra is switching roles and becoming a support hero. 

Sombra’s been a tough nut to crack for Overwatch, often overpowered at the highly coordinated pro level, and annoying to both teammates and opponents at the casual level — largely due to her ability to go invisible and quickly teleport across the map. She’s already been through four reworks by my count, and the devs seem to make smaller-but-still-substantial tweaks to her kit every six months or so. As a longtime support player and Sombra-enjoyer (which I will not apologize for), I’m very excited for this change.

Roadhog’s also getting a rework, although he’s staying within the tank role. Like Sombra, he’s a hero who’s been a longtime annoyance for players, due largely to being balanced around a hook ability that can quickly combo down non-tank heroes.

Hearthstone announces next expansion, new class coming next year

Blizzard’s card battler is taking players back 10,000 years in the past with the upcoming Reign of the Black Empire expansion, which adds a new “assemble” keyword allowing players to smush two minions’ text boxes together. It’s also getting a new Journey feature that will be a dedicated home for events, story content and limited-time events.

In March, the game will also add its first new hero in six years: the monk. Blizzard didn’t say much about the new class, but I’m sure we’ll hear more about it over the course of BlizzCon.

New content for Heroes of the Storm

Heroes of the Storm is getting a new hero for the first time in six years. Xal’atath from World of Warcraft is joining the roster later this month. The multiplayer online battle arena has been largely in maintenance mode since 2022, though still receiving periodic balance patches. Whether the new hero marks the start of more dedicated support for the game likely depends on how much interest it generates.

 

This is a developing story and will be updated as Blizzard releases more information.

Editors’ note: Adam Benjamin’s travel costs for BlizzCon were covered by Blizzard Entertainment. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

title: Apple nailed iPhone Duo split screen, even as iPad multitasking feels convoluted
snippet: Apple this week unveiled its new iPhone lineup, including the first ever foldable iPhone – the iPhone Duo. While the Duo itself is a fantastic device, it does leave me wishing that Apple did better for the iPad. more…
fullText:
Apple this week unveiled its new iPhone lineup, including the first ever foldable iPhone – the iPhone Duo. While the Duo itself is a fantastic device, it does leave me wishing that Apple did better for the iPad.

Ever since the release of iPadOS 26 last year, I’ve missed the earlier days of iPad multitasking. Sure, windowing is cool – but I don’t want that all the time. With iPadOS 26, you’re either all in on windowing, or you can only use apps in full screen. Apple did re-introduce split screen and slideover in later versions, but the features still require you to utilize the windowing system.

With iPhone Duo, multitasking feels much more elegant. You can put an app into half of a splitscreen, whilst still seeing your full home screen to select another app. You can also save apps as a pair for swapping into later. iPhone Duo also offers something no iPad offers, the ability to splitscreen a video with an app. On iPad mini, which is very similarly sized to iPhone Duo, this could be excellent.

And yet, iPadOS 27 still takes an all or nothing approach to multitasking. Even on the iPad mini where windowing is far too convoluted.

	

iPhone Duo offers a vision for how nice multitasking could be on the iPad. I’m not saying we should take away windowing, but if Apple has already engineered a simpler multitasking system, why not bring it to the iPad. At its core, iPadOS is still iOS, and while not everything can automatically scale to the iPad, it shouldn’t be a massive undertaking.

Personally, I’m incredibly excited for the iPhone Duo. Apple nailed the software implementation in a manner that nobody was really thinking about, but in hindsight its such an obvious direction for the future of foldables. I just wish Apple didn’t make iPad multitasking borderline hostile towards those of us who aren’t using a Magic Keyboard.

title: iPhone Duo can add fake bezel to the outside screen for better case compatibility
snippet: Blogger Nicolas Lellouche went digging in the iPhone Duo settings during his hands on time with the device. He found a curious new option in the display settings called ‘Shift Left Edge’. When enabled, this setting adds a bit of a black border to the left side, essentially adding fake bezel on the outside screen, pushing content away from the folding edge. more…
fullText:
Blogger Nicolas Lellouche went digging in the iPhone Duo settings during his hands on time with the device. He found a curious new option in the display settings called ‘Shift Left Edge’. 

When enabled, this setting adds a bit of a black border to the left side, essentially adding fake bezel on the outside screen, pushing content away from the folding edge.

The description for this setting in the iPhone Duo software says that it “moves content when you are using a case that partially covers the left edge of the outer display of your iPhone”.

As you can see from his short demo video, with the setting turned on, it roughly doubles the width of the black border on the left edge of the iPhone’s Duo outer screen. 

It’s unclear what kind of cases would require this setting to be enabled. 

Apple is offering two first-party case accessories for the iPhone Duo at launch; the iPhone Duo Case and the iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand. 

Without having proper hands on time, it’s hard to tell whether these cases significantly overlap the left edge and obscure the screen content, but it doesn’t seem like it would be an issue. It is possible Apple is envisaging this setting will be useful for other — perhaps more rugged — case designs offered by third-party accessory makers.

We’ll know more closer to launch. iPhone Duo goes on sale next month, on October 23rd.

title: Hands-on: Orbitkey elevated its time-tested key organizer with a built-in Google Find Hub tracker
snippet: If you happen to walk past the Orbitkey’s setup at IFA in Berlin, you might have seen what the company is known for — key organizers. You’d be forgiven for not thinking these new key organizers had Google Find Hub trackers built in. more…
fullText:
If you happen to walk past the Orbitkey’s setup at IFA in Berlin, you might have seen what the company is known for — key organizers. You’d be forgiven for not thinking these new key organizers had Google Find Hub trackers built in.

Orbitkey isn’t new to Google Find Hub trackers, and certainly not key organizers. But its brand-new Key Organizer Tracker is the culmination of both, blending the visual design of what makes the company’s popular key holders so popular with more utility. I spent some time during IFA with the new key tool, and it’s already part of my EDC going forward.

The Key Organizer Tracker works with both Google Find Hub and Apple Find My networks by keeping a built-in tracker tucked in one of the sides. It looks thick at first glance, but I found that the new tracker/organizer is no thicker than some key-keepers, like the Ridge version I was lugging around. If your key organizer has a belt clip, Orbitkey’s Key Organizer Tracker will take up just as much space.

I’ve been using it for a few days during my IFA trip, and even though I don’t need to pull out my keys while on the go, I’ve toyed around with it enough to appreciate the design. Keys stay tucked and don’t spin, and the post has a semi-locking mechanism that prevents the keeper from loosening unnecessarily. Instead of a piece of spring steel sticking out to keep friction on your keys, Orbitkey uses a patented pressure ring that provides the perfect amount of pushback to keep them from spinning or locking in place.

	

Even the bottom key ring made for accompanying car keys is designed well. It’s fixed at the bottom, where the leather and plastic bend around. It doesn’t slide up into the space where keys sit, which makes pulling it out and grabbing the right key easier.

The tracker itself is no-nonsense, which is perfect. There’s a button for pairing and an LED to indicate status. It has a speaker to play loud chirps through the Google Find Hub app, and it charges via a magnetic pin charger included with the organizer. Orbitkey says the new Key Organizer Tracker lasts for 3-5 months, depending on your use. With how easy it is to charge, even with keys on it, that’s a respectable length of time.

Fit and finish feel great, as well. It has a faux-leather outer layer in tons of color options, and the rest of the keyboard’s build is made of sturdy, quality plastic.

Orbitkey also announced a new standalone tracker to complement the key holder. It’s shaped like a small popsicle stick, so it might not fit in your AirTag-branded accessories. Still, I’ve found it sort of slips into just about any bag. In Orbitkey’s new tech pouches, it fits into a dedicated pocket, so it won’t get lost in the clutter.

It has the same specs as the key tracker, with 3-5 months of battery and the same charging method.

Both the Orbitkey Key Organizer Tracker and the standalone Tracker come in a bunch of colors. Even though my pictures only show the black colorway, the rest of the company’s color options are vibrant. The key organizer comes in Black, Blush, Cobalt, Citrus, and Orange leather-free options. Leather versions come in Black, Tan, and Forest.

The Orbitkey Key Organizer Tracker starts at $69.90, and the Universal Tracker starts at $34.90. Both are on sale now, and the Key Organizer Tracker is currently available for pre-order.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 display corners can bend inward on purpose, Samsung says [Gallery]
snippet: The internet is mad. Shocking statement, I know, but this time it’s about a perceived quality control issue on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 that sees the display corners able to bend or flex inward, but that Samsung says is part of the design. more…
fullText:
The internet is mad. Shocking statement, I know, but this time it’s about a perceived quality control issue on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 that sees the display corners able to bend or flex inward, but that Samsung says is part of the design.

On Reddit, Samsung’s forums, and endless social media posts – as well as a heaping pile of clickbaity headlines – a “flaw” with the Fold 8 is being criticized. Some have noticed that when you apply pressure to the corner of the inner display on Samsung’s new foldable, the corner flexes inward, leaving a small gap between the display and the bezel until the pressure is released. It seems to be more pronounced on some devices rather than others – on my personal Fold 8, it’s barely noticeable.

Reactions have varied, with one thread calling on Samsung to recall the device due to this.

Via @TheGalox_
Via Samsung forums

Samsung says, though, that this is normal behavior.

	

In a statement to Business Post as well as a reply apparently through its forums, Samsung explains that the corners of the display flex to protect the display in the case that something is trapped within the folded display, as well as to “reduce the impact of interference or pressure between internal components of the display.” The statement explains:

If something like sand adheres to the top surface of the internal display, the screen could get scratched when the Fold is folded. We designed it so the display indents slightly to provide a cushioning effect and prevent damage. Since this feature was prepared to ensure consumers do not experience inconvenience, we have not provided a separate official explanation.

One of the main concerns here was in regards to water resistance, with many assuming that this gap would let water get into the internals of the device. This was tested directly by one user, who applied pressure to the display corners while the Fold 8 was entirely submerged in water, with the foldable coming out unscathed. 

What do you think?

title: The iPhone Duo Isn’t the Pocket iPad… or Is It?
snippet: Commentary: I can’t figure out if the Duo would replace my iPad, or if it’s just a portable alternative.
fullText:
I’m having deja vu after Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event, which introduced the company’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo. It’s on two levels: Back in 2020, Microsoft introduced its take on a folding phone, also called the Duo. I remember talking about it with Panos Panay, at that time Microsoft’s chief product officer, and realizing that a hinged, dual-screen phone was in some ways the phone of my dreams, but not in all the ways I wanted.

But that’s not all. I’m writing these thoughts about the iPhone Duo on a Magic Keyboard-equipped iPad Air that sometimes — but not always — replaces my MacBook. I’m having similar feelings about the iPhone Duo and the iPad.

Could the Duo be the iPad-to-go of my dreams? Could it easily evolve to meet my needs? Or would I still find myself wishing to go back to the iPad sometimes?

	

			

Not quite an iPad

Apple has a knack for expanding and blending its product lines while approaching, but never reaching, a place where one actually replaces the other. A case in point: The iPad’s decade-plus evolution to a device that can feel uncannily Mac-like at times, yet still not be a Mac.

I’m getting the same vibes from the iPhone Duo. The device is “inspired by the versatility of iPad,” according to Apple, but it’s not actually an iPad. 

Unfolded on a table, it looks like an iPad.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

And yet, iPad Mini-like

I felt excitement about the iPhone Duo as I watched the news literally unfold. I haven’t cared about many folding phones because they either didn’t seem like true tablets or they looked pocket-unfriendly. The iPhone Duo’s size seems right, and its aspect ratios and design remind me of an iPad Mini. 

But also, it supports the Apple Pencil! And it can run some split-screen apps in ways that look like an iPad. Could iPad apps, of which I have tons already, run on this too? Would this be a way to have the best of both worlds in my pocket for a breathtaking $1,999-and-up price?

I’m curious how well the Duo handles the Pencil. The iPad Mini supports the Pencil Pro, but the Duo doesn’t.Josh Goldman/CNET

What it still seems to lack

The Duo doesn’t run iPadOS. Its iOS variant has what looks like a different layout, with side-oriented menus and docks, repositioned notification indicators, different layout orientations for apps, and a focus on continuity between single and dual-screen views of the same apps when folded and unfolded. 

The Pencil support is for the USB-C Pencil, not any of the Pencil 2 or Pencil Pros, which have advanced pressure sensitivity, hovering input features and gyro-enabled brushes. And I’d need to carry that Pencil around in my pocket or some sort of future Pencil-enabled case, since Apple didn’t announce a tinier Pencil that could connect with the Duo.

And as I type up this story on an iPad keyboard, I wonder how well the Duo supports keyboard accessories or windowed layouts that could give me the workspace that iPads can. Possibly? I’m sure I could pair a keyboard, for instance. But would it feel good? Or would I even want it?

You can get a lot of other Apple devices for the Duo’s $2,000 price tag. Or, at least, two.Patrick Holland/CNET

A price difference

I also wonder whether the Duo would replace an iPad Mini, which it clearly looks set up to do. The iPad Mini is far less expensive, starting at just $599. There’s another OLED-screened model expected this fall, maybe at the same time as the iPhone Duo, which arrives Oct. 23. You could buy an iPad Mini and an iPhone 18 Pro for less than the cost of an iPhone Duo.

But not that much less. You’d be spending at least $1,798 compared to the Duo’s $1,999 base price.

Alternatively, a basic iPad and an entry iPhone 17E would collectively cost $1,148.

So the Duo doesn’t make sense, right? Unless it can be both? Would it be both? Or would I suddenly have two iPad-like devices, one for my pocket, one for my home?

Could the Duo’s design influence future iPads?Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

A sign of things to come from Apple?

I’m a little annoyed that the Duo isn’t entirely an iPad, but why do I feel less upset than I do about the iPad not fully being a Mac? It might be because the iPad itself has always been a bridge device, something that’s a bit iPhone, a bit Mac. 

I have a feeling that the Duo’s destiny isn’t set in stone, that this phone will transform into new forms and accessory uses. It might even become a dockable computer. After all, didn’t new CEO John Ternus reframe the iPhone as an intelligent hub? Am I hallucinating? Dreaming stupid dreams? Perhaps. Sometimes a decade can pass while you’re waiting for Apple to do something it never does.

Microsoft’s Surface Duo disappeared from the market after just a few short years, around the same time that Microsoft’s broader Windows Phone ambitions – merging the worlds of phone and desktop designs and functionality – turned to dust. 

In 2026, the iPhone Duo will not be a full iPad. But maybe this new melting identity of the iPhone is a sign that all product categories are starting to flex. Even the iPad. I just wonder if the Duo’s going to feel like it’s truly the best of both worlds, or if I’d still prefer going back to an iPad after all.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein
						

						

							Editor at Large						
					

											

								

											I started with CNET reviewing laptops in 2009. Now I explore wearable tech, VR/AR, tablets, gaming and future/emerging trends in our changing world. Other obsessions include magic, immersive theater, puzzles, board games, cooking, improv and the New York Jets. My background includes an MFA in theater which I apply to thinking about immersive experiences of the future.

title: Apple hid a classic Mac easter egg in the iOS 27 Settings app
snippet: Many have complained that Apple design has been sapped of some of its trademark whimsy in recent years. Well, here’s the latest example of how the tides seem to be changing. Buried in the Settings app on iOS 27, Apple has hidden an easter egg that hails back from classic Mac OS; Clarus the Dogcow. Here’s how to trigger it … more…
fullText:
Many have complained that Apple design has been sapped of some of its trademark whimsy in recent years. Well, here’s the latest example of how the tides seem to be changing. 

Buried in the Settings app on iOS 27, Apple has hidden an easter egg that hails back from classic Mac OS; Clarus the Dogcow. Here’s how to trigger it …

iOS 27 includes a new feature that lets user customize the intensity of the Liquid Glass transparency effects, with a slider ranging from Clear to fully Tinted. You can find that setting on your iPhone by going to Settings -> Appearance -> Liquid Glass. 

In this pane, Apple includes some faux website user interface so you can preview how the Liquid Glass appearance changes as you adjust the slider. There’s a little scrollable region including some text and photography from Apple Park. 

Here’s where the easter egg comes in: scroll all the way to the bottom and keep pulling up with your finger and it will reveal a photo of a Clarus the Dogcow figurine next to the Apple Park pond. Rainbow text reading ‘Moof!’, the noise a dogcow makes, also appears in the example search text field. 

And if you type ‘Moof!’ to Siri in Spotlight, it will even reply “Nice dogcow.”.

For those unfamiliar with the history, Clarus the Dogcow relates back to an icon created by Susan Kare for the original Mac, as a glyph for the Cairo font (the classic Mac’s icon font, similar to Windows’ Dingbats). It has essentially no utility; it’s just a bit of fun.

You can also find the same easter egg on MacOS Golden Gate in the Appearance menu of the System Settings app.

Still rolling out (beta)

These are Messages features that Google announced or have been spotted in the wild by beta users.

Customizable attachments grid

Google is testing two designs, with the one on the right taking up more of your screen.

	

Learn more

Instead of a top toolbar, long-pressing on a message or image opens a floating menu as the background blurs. Another press lets you copy just a part of the chat. Previously, you had to copy the entire message.

Learn more

When iOS 27 launches this fall, Android-iPhone conversations over RCS will gain support for inline replies that include quotes, as well as photo reactions with the actual emoji instead of just the text description. This feature is currently in beta.

title: Samsung is shutting down ‘Quick Measure’ and ‘AR Doodle’ apps for Galaxy phones
snippet: Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year. more…
fullText:
Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year.

Confirmed in Galaxy Store listings for both the “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” apps, Samsung will be shutting down these AR experiences on December 31, 2026. Samsung explains that both will be “returning with improved services in the future.”

“Quick Measure” is an AR app that lets you get measurements of real-world distance from your phone, while “AR Doodle” lets you “draw” on real-world locations through the camera app.

The shutdown will block new downloads of both apps, while also pulling the plug on any future updates. The app won’t just stop working immediately, but any OS updates will break the apps in time. Notably, Samsung seems to have hidden both app listings on the latest One UI versions, making them inivisible in the Galaxy Store.

	

Samsung says:

Please be advised that service for the Quick measure app is scheduled to be terminated on 31 December 2026.

After this date, new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it is already downloaded, but please be aware that some features may not function properly.

Additionally, compatibility support for the Quick measure app will no longer be provided for future OS updates.

We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause and thank all our customers for their loyal use of the Quick measure app. We are committed to returning with improved services in the future.

It’s unclear when these replacement apps might arrive, but it’s certainly a shame to see these going away.

title: Craig Federighi addresses iPhone Duo and iPad overlap
snippet: Craig Federighi, Apple’s senior vice president of Software Engineering, sat down with MKBHD this week to talk about the new iPhone Duo. In the interview, Federighi talked about the potential overlap between the iPhone Duo and an iPad. more…
fullText:
Sc			
	

Craig Federighi, Apple’s senior vice president of Software Engineering, sat down with MKBHD this week to talk about the new iPhone Duo. In the interview, Federighi talked about the potential overlap between the iPhone Duo and an iPad.

Craig Federighi: iPad vs iPhone Duo

Federighi likened the situation to the iPad and Mac, where people ultimately fell into “very natural patterns” deciding between when to use their iPad and when to use their Mac. Federighi believes the same pattern will play out between the iPad and iPhone Duo,

He did, however, particularly call out the iPad mini as a potential overlap with the iPhone Duo:

“I find in my usage over the last few months, if I am starting on the iPhone, I happen to sit down, and I actually just want to go deeper into a piece of content, I want to read something, this device is extraordinary to open up, often in portrait actually, and page through some content. It’s fantastic. I think people are going to find their way.

But I agree, for someone who maybe had an iPad mini or something, this device can often fill that space for them.”

As you might expect from a software engineering executive, Federighi also called out the lengths Apple went to adapt the iOS experience to the iPhone Duo—especially compared with the competition.

“I think on a lot of other devices, it’s been, ‘We’re just going to stretch out or cram some other experience into whatever the new form factor is.’ For us, this was like, ‘This whole thing, we’re going to design it right from the start,’” Federighi explained.

title: Automattic confirms Mullenweg has returned as CEO after attempted ouster by board
snippet: Automattic says Mullenweg is back as "chairman and CEO of Automattic, with full support of the board."
fullText:
After a tumultuous week that saw WordPress founder Matt Mullenweg ousted from his position as CEO of WordPress.com’s parent company Automattic by way of a board vote, the company has now issued a statement confirming that Mullenweg has returned to his position.

“Matt Mullenweg is the chairman and CEO of Automattic, with full support of the board and if you search online you can see many top executives and Automatticians supporting him as well,” a company spokesperson shared with TechCrunch via email just after 5 p.m. ET on Saturday evening. (The mention of online support appears to refer to supportive posts on X that Mullenweg has been reposting from his X account.)

Automattic’s board had voted earlier this week to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence for unknown reasons. The move seemingly came as a surprise to Mullenweg, who posted on Automattic’s Slack, accusing the board members of “conspiring” against him. 

Automattic confirmed Mullenweg’s removal to TechCrunch on Wednesday, saying that Mullenweg was “currently on leave” and that Automattic’s chief financial officer, Mark Davies, would lead as interim CEO with “full confidence” of the board.

However, the board’s plan did not go smoothly. Seemingly declining to depart, Mullenweg booted other admins out of the company Slack and told employees everything had been worked out and that he was back in control of Automattic, multiple sources told TechCrunch. At one point, he also posted to Slack, “I’m a pirate now” and cursed, which is something Mullenweg famously did not do. “If this is an HR problem, please wrangle me in since my normal wranglers are with Mark Davies,” he wrote.

When TechCrunch asked Mullenweg if his comments about being back as CEO were legitimate, he promised a blog post was coming. When it arrived, however, it was about him buying a houseboat. When we asked if his comments about being back were also him trolling, he replied, “I’m not a troll I’m a pirate, obviously.” Mullenweg never provided any official comment about his return, but noted on X that this was likely the fifth time he’s faced a “coup.”

Automattic also did not respond to repeated requests for comment on Friday, nor to reports we heard about board member Toni Schneider stepping down. Schneider, a founding CEO of Automattic, now leads Bluesky. He did not return requests for comment at his personal email or via requests sent to Bluesky. 

We have since asked Automattic again about this and other changes to the board’s composition, which we’re hearing still may be in flux. 

The company responded to our questions about board composition after publication early on Monday morning, with the following statement: “Matt and Automattic’s leadership team have great respect for everyone involved. While we can’t comment on specific individuals, we’re thankful for their contributions to Automattic and its mission, and we remain excited about what’s ahead with Matt at the helm. Matt was away for only 33 hours and 20 minutes—we’re now back to work.”

fullText:
KeySmart might make one of the best-designed Android Find Hub trackers in the shape of a credit card, and it’s down to $38 right now.

The KeySmart SmartCard is one of the best form factors in a tracker. It’s the size of a credit card, so it fits in any regular or passport wallet, and it’s thin enough to slide between your things in a backpack. Down from $45, the KeySmart SmartCard Gen 3 is currently $37.99 on Amazon. It’s not the biggest discount we’ve seen, but it’s a solid little chunk off of a device that’s well worth it at full value. We’re not sure how long this deal will last.

title: Google details ADB Wi-Fi 2.0 for more reliable wireless Android debugging
snippet: Available as a part of Android 17, Google is making wireless debugging a whole lot more reliable with ADB Wi-Fi 2.0. more…
fullText:
Available as a part of Android 17, Google is making wireless debugging a whole lot more reliable with ADB Wi-Fi 2.0. 

Wireless debugging has been around in Android for quite some time now, but it’s not always been the most reliable offering. Between more complex pairing and general hiccups in usability, wired has still been the primary choice for many. 

Google is aiming to fix that with ADB Wi-Fi 2.0. In a post, Google details what has changed with the new process, explaining three core updates:

A new server stack (adb): Previously, wireless device connections would sever when network configurations changed or devices were turned off. This meant that connections would drop for common occurrences. With our new mDNS stack, we’ve replaced both Bonjour and legacy mDNS so that your wireless devices more reliably stay connected as you go about your day.

Smarter network handling (adbd): Previously, the workstation’s mDNS client would sporadically drop services. Now, the daemon automatically turns off ADB Wi-Fi when it detects an untrusted network and re-enables itself once running on a user-allowed network.

Improved discoverability in Android Studio: Previously, Wi-Fi pairing was difficult to find. Now, you simply enable wireless debugging on your phone and it will show in Android Studio’s Device Manager.

Google says that these changes have made auto-connect around 32% more reliable, while connections are 66% faster for roughly 90% of connections tested. 

	

For Android Studio, wireless debugging can be used via the “pair over Wi-Fi” button, with a QR code connecting your device to your computer for an ADB connection.

title: The race to build great iPhone Duo apps is about to begin
snippet: When iPhone Duo arrives next month, many third-party apps might not work as well as Apple’s built-in apps. There’s a reason for that, at least initially, though the situation should improve over time. more…
fullText:
When iPhone Duo arrives next month, many third-party apps might not work as well as Apple’s built-in apps. There’s a reason for that, at least initially, though the situation should improve over time.

Three levels of iPhone Duo app support

We shared a look yesterday at how third-party software will work with iPhone Duo. There are three compatibility levels. Apps built for iOS 26 and earlier run in a mode that doesn’t take advantage of the larger display at all. If Apple released the iPhone Duo today, this is how all third-party apps would look.

iOS 27 comes out on Monday, though, and Apple is now accepting app submissions built for the new operating system. iPhone apps built for iOS 27 look much more at home on iPhone Duo. There’s still unused screen space, but it’s not nearly as rough as the other compatibility mode.

Then there’s full iPhone Duo app compatibility. This mode will see apps take full advantage of the iPhone Duo display, including moving controls previously in toolbars previously at the top over to the side.

Standard apps get a head start

If an app uses standard system controls without any custom work around toolbars and navigation bars, this mode will be what you can expect when iPhone Duo ships.

However, it’s very common for apps to use custom solutions for toolbars and navbars. Just take a look at apps that you frequently use. If they don’t look like Apple’s stock apps, there’s a good chance that they’re doing custom work in their app that won’t automatically translate.

For that reason, these kinds of apps will require a lot more work than just building against the iOS 27.1 SDK. The “automatic” compatibility really only works for apps that are strictly standard and already follow Apple’s layout suggestions without deviating at all. 

The race begins (soon, but not yet) with new developer tools

The good news is that Apple will provide developers with tools to prepare their apps for the iPhone Duo before it reaches customers next month. The bad news is that this work can’t start yet.

Apple will need to release a new version of Xcode and the first iOS 27.1 developer beta before developers can test their apps. This will provide a virtual iPhone Duo through Xcode’s simulator, which will help with initial support. However, most developers won’t have access to a real iPhone Duo until launch day. 

And for apps that do a lot of custom layout work, iPhone Duo software optimization will likely be a longer road. And that’s before any considerations for all the special modes that the iPhone Duo supports. 

A valuable new audience for developers

But while the iPhone Duo will be niche to start, it’s also an iPhone and not a virtual reality headset or a specialized version of an otherwise specialized product.

iPhone Duo’s $2000 starting price also means that app developers can expect Duo users to be more likely to spend on the App Store. Prioritizing software updates for Duo customers might just be good business.

Still, iPhone Duo optimizations for major social media apps, banking apps, and any number of games? That will be a big area to watch over the next several months. Just don’t expect everything to be perfectly prepared on day one.

Given how new and ambitious iPhone Duo is in terms of iOS layout and features, we should expect it to be a rare gem to celebrate when a third-party app ships a great iPhone Duo app — at least for the first several months. 

iPhone Duo will start arriving to customers on October 23. Pre-orders begin October 16.

title: The iPhone Duo is Apple at its absolute best (and a little bit at its worst)
snippet: Wow. After Samsung had a seven-year head start on Apple in the foldables market, the company really had to live up to its ethos of waiting until it could do a far better job than everyone else, and boy did it deliver with the iPhone Duo! It was abundantly clear that Apple had thought through every detail of what a foldable iPhone needed to be, and has taken advantage of every benefit the form factor has to offer … more…
fullText:
Wow. After Samsung had a seven-year head start on Apple in the foldables market, the company really had to live up to its ethos of waiting until it could do a far better job than everyone else, and boy did it deliver with the iPhone Duo!

It was abundantly clear that Apple had thought through every detail of what a foldable iPhone needed to be, and has taken advantage of every benefit the form factor has to offer …

It starts with the basics. Prior reports talked about Apple waiting until it could make the crease virtually invisible and ensure the hinge design would be robust enough to survive endless cycles of folding and unfolding, and while the latter remains to be seen, we can already see the work that went into that hinge design.

There’s the under-screen front-facing camera that’s visible when you need it and almost invisible when you don’t.

Apple also thought about all of the different ways in which the device could be held or positioned, and how the software could best take advantage of that.

I’m not sure who first said it, but I think it’s absolutely true that great design is something no-one else thought of, yet looks blindingly obvious in hindsight. The OG iPhone was a great example of this. Other smartphones had physical keyboards and required* a stylus to use them, while the iPhone is used with your finger and a keyboard only appears when it’s required. It was obvious afterwards that of course smartphones should work this way.

*Yes, the Duo supports the Apple Pencil, but it doesn’t require one.

For me, there were plenty of examples of this in the Duo presentation. Why should we need to first isolate a subject in a photo and then copy it into another app when we could simply drag it there directly from the original photo? That’s completely obvious after the fact.

Replacing a camera self-timer with the device simply waiting until everyone stops moving and then taking the photo automatically. Obvious!

	

Then there were the UI features that have no reason to exist but simply look beautiful, like that blurring effect as you fold the phone.

I could go on at some length, but the bottom line is that I had extremely high expectations for this device yet was still blown away by just how good it appears to be. I’m British; the only time we ever use the word “wow” is sarcastically – but I still had to open this piece with it, without a trace of sarcasm.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo. 

And that brings me to that “little bit the worst of Apple” remark in the headline. The company has the ability to create product videos that make us feel we can reach out through the screen and touch the device. Apple can create strong desire for a product we have absolutely no business buying. I’m not the target market for the iPhone Duo, but I do, absolutely, unquestionably want one. How about you?

title: Apple’s New iPhone Duo Folds Horizontally, Like a Passport
snippet: It’s like you’re opening a small book, not flipping a Star Trek communicator open. And the crease marking where it folds is almost invisible.
fullText:
If you’re used to the vertical flip opening of phones like the Motorola Razr, or still fondly remember snapping your vintage not-so-smart cellphone open and shut, think different. The just-announced folding iPhone Duo opens horizontally, like a book, and its size and fold direction make it reminiscent of a paper passport. The much-anticipated phone was revealed Wednesday at Apple’s latest event.

While it wasn’t confirmed until this week, the folding phone was the worst-kept secret in tech, with hundreds of articles reporting that it was on the way. And it joins a crowded field of foldable phones, with key players including Samsung, Google and Motorola, and Chinese brands like Honor, Oppo and Huawei. But as CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti notes, Apple’s entry into the fray is expected to nudge foldable phone designs forward.

Al-Heeti notes that the iPhone Duo is compact, and Apple says it’s the thinnest iPhone ever when opened. The phone has a 7.6-inch display on the inside, a 5.4-inch outer display, and will come in two colors,  star white and night sky.

	

			

Foldable phones typically have visible creases where the phones fold in half. CNET Director of Content Patrick Holland notes that this is an issue preventing some shoppers from buying foldable phones, but he says the crease is “nearly nonexistent” on the iPhone Duo. He says it will be interesting to see whether the crease becomes more pronounced as the foldable phone ages, as it has with all other foldable phones.

title: Google Pixel Tablet has been discontinued, out of stock everywhere
snippet: The Pixel Tablet is done, as Google has officially pulled the plug on the slate by entirely deleting the listing on its store. more…
fullText:
The Pixel Tablet is done, as Google has officially pulled the plug on the slate by entirely deleting the listing on its store.

Google launched the Pixel Tablet in 2023 as a hybrid of a typical Android tablet and a Nest Hub smart display. It was met with mixed reactions, but still serves as the only tablet in Google’s lineup. 

And now it’s done.

While updates are set to continue through 2028, Google has quietly removed the Pixel Tablet from its Store. A direct link to the listing now redirects to the homepage, while there’s also no mention of the Pixel Tablet anywhere on the Google Store besides a few accessories that remain. The change was spotted by Jetstream earlier today. 

	

Sales of the Pixel Tablet closed up in late August (thanks Noah!), but the listing was still working roughly a week ago – we checked it when Nest prices went up, and the Tablet was still listed as out of stock at the time (August 31). It’s the same old pattern, a device goes out of stock before being removed from the store. Generally speaking, removing the device from its store is Google’s way of marking a device as discontinued – another recent example would be Nest Mini and Nest Audio, which were removed and confirmed as discontinued not long after going out of stock. 

Google never did ship a Pixel Tablet sequel, with rumors of some big upgrades being canceled over profitability concerns. Had a sequel continued on, it allegedly would have arrived in 2025, with a third-gen release in 2027 that was also shelved.

	

While third-party retailers often have stock left over when Google ends its own sales of a product, Pixel Tablet is out of stock everywhere we’ve looked. Amazon doesn’t even have any third-party sellers with stock left.

RIP.

title: Motorola teases wide Razr Fold as its ‘next move’ in response to iPhone Duo debut
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo announcement has triggered a couple of companies, and it’s apparently warranted at least one teaser for even more foldables. This one seems to be a wide version of the Motorola Razr Fold. more…
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo announcement has triggered a couple of companies, and it’s apparently warranted at least one teaser for even more foldables. This one seems to be a wide version of the Motorola Razr Fold.

After years of watching manufacturers improve on the concept of a foldable phone, Apple has a genuine answer – the iPhone Duo. In a lot of respects, it looks like the original Pixel Fold. But software seems to be a heavy selling point, with plenty of tricks and touches that sell the idea of an iOS-powered foldable.

The fallout has been interesting. Samsung’s team took to Twitter/X to acknowledge Apple’s release, with a slew of posts that almost seem clingy. They didn’t have anything solid to offer, though. But Motorola did.

The mobile company responsible for the Razr of years past and the Razr foldables current posted a snarky little video on Instagram in response to the iPhone Duo’s existence. A series of shots shows Razr phones spanning back a few generations snapping shut. The iconic pink Motorola Razr flip phone starts it off. The last recognizable phone in the video is a Motorola Razr Fold, which launched earlier this year.

	

Right after that, the video ends with a blacked-out foldable that resembles the iPhone Duo’s short and stout nature. It’s not Apple’s new release, but it’s possible it could be a wide Razr Fold from Motorola. In the post, Motorola calls it its “next move,” which seems telling enough.

If our eyes can be trusted, there are a couple of details to pick out for what could be a wide Motorola Razr Fold. The camera bar spans the entire width of the phone’s rear panel. A button can also be seen on the top left of the inner display view. The iPhone Duo has two volume rockers on the right side.

It’s just a silhouette, and those little details could prove to be completely off. But Motorola isn’t ready to say what the device is, or when it will launch. It simply wants users to know it exists since the hype for short and wide foldables seems to be growing, thanks to Samsung and now Apple.

title: Samsung reacts to Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo; ‘reheating our leftovers’
snippet: Samsung is apparently of two minds when it comes to reacting to Apple’s first foldable device, with some interesting reactions to the iPhone Duo’s unveiling, calling the device “a Sims sequel” and “reheating our leftovers.” more…
fullText:
Samsung is apparently of two minds when it comes to reacting to Apple’s first foldable device, with some interesting reactions to the iPhone Duo’s unveiling, calling the device “a Sims sequel” and “reheating our leftovers.”

Apple’s first foldable is official, with the iPhone Duo sharing a form factor similar to that of Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8. Samsung’s device has been very well received since its debut in July, though one could argue that the new shape was somewhat of a reaction to Apple’s imminent arrival on the scene. Chicken or egg, your choice, but Samsung’s public reaction has been quite something to watch.

The foldable pioneer was welcoming to Apple ahead of the launch, but the Twitter/X feed tells another story. Samsung called the iPhone Duo a “Sim sequel” and “So far, so same,” referring to how much of what the iPhone Duo can do has been seen on existing Android foldables, including Galaxy Z Fold 8. 

Samsung further poked fun at Apple only having one foldable form factor and, for whatever reason, took issue with the idea of using the Duo as a clock, but also called the iPhone Duo a case of “reheating our leftovers.” 

	

Let us know when you're done reheating our leftovers 😉

— Samsung Mobile US (@SamsungMobileUS) September 9, 2026

	

Bold statement given the complete 180-degree turn the Fold 8’s design is compared to Samsung’s long history of book-style foldables. Surely a coincidence, but I digress. 

Samsung even pulled Duolingo into the conversation to poke fun at Apple’s branding – Duolingo itself had already done – with Duolingo replying to call Samsung an “ugly stranger” in reference to a viral meme.

Apple’s iPhone Duo launches in October for $1,999.

title: Boox Picco is exceptionally tiny for an e-reader, but it parts ways with Android and third-party apps
snippet: Boox offered some wandering the halls of Messe Berlin at IFA 2026 the opportunity to check out its most exciting upcoming release – a tiny e-reader called the “Picco” that you could probably pocket and take anywhere. more…
fullText:
Boox offered some wandering the halls of Messe Berlin at IFA 2026 the opportunity to check out its most exciting upcoming release – a tiny e-reader called the “Picco” that you could probably pocket and take anywhere.

Boox laid out a product trajectory over the last few years that builds on Android to offer an e-reader experience open to third-party apps. That includes Google Play Books, Kindle, and so much more.

The Boox Picco, which is slated for a November release, won’t offer that experience.

Instead, this e-reader experience hinges on a “take anywhere” design coming in at somewhere just under 4 inches. At that size, it’s the ultimate travel e-reader if you’re ok with a rather small viewing area.

	

It’s garnered a lot of hype for an e-reader, and it deserves a lot of it. It’s small, thin, and has some of Boox’s best features, like an adjustable front light for reading at any time of the day. It even has a set of custom buttons and page rockers built specifically for an easy experience.

Related: The Boox Go 10.3 Gen II is as massive as it is minimal, and I love that for it

But the Boox Picco won’t run Android, and that feels like a big loss. Android e-readers, like much of the company’s backlog, allow users to install third-party apps beyond what the OS offers. In essence, it opens the doors to your existing libraries you’ve built over time from apps like Kindle or Google Play Books. Without those apps, you’re left with the Boox store and epub files.

The Picco will come with a companion app that lets users transfer files to the reader, and even though what we got hands-on time with was an early unit, it seemed like a solid system. But this leaves you limited on options, and you’ll have to find epub versions of your favorite stories and publications.

You might also be disappointed if you were expecting MagSafe compatibility or Qi2.2 support to get it to stick to the back of your phone.

I can’t let that entirely detract from the absolutely adorable e-reader. The early unit we played around with felt great in hand, and even with a tiny screen, I can see plenty of uses for such a small device. It’s essentially the size of a mini field journal, and carrying it on you in your bag or even pocket all day is a no-brainer if you know you’ll get some downtime to catch up on a book or two.

The lack of Android probably also facilitates a more compelling price. Boox says the device will be listed for somewhere around $100, though no details are final. If the Boox Picco hits that price tag and the experience is as easy as it seems it will be, the Picco might deserve every bit of praise it’s getting before it’s even released.

Boox plans to launch the Picco sometime in November.

title: Google Photos trash bin now deletes media after 30 days, down from 60 days
snippet: Google Photos has updated its trash bin timeline, cutting the time from 60 days to 30 days as of September 2026. more…
fullText:
Google Photos has updated its trash bin timeline, cutting the time from 60 days to 30 days as of September 2026.

The trash bin in Google Photos gives users a chance to recover deleted photos and videos for a limited period of time. That period was 60 days for the longest time, effectively giving users about two months to recover anything that might have been deleted by accident or simply needed to be recovered. 

Google has now cut that to 30 days.

The change is rolling out now, as noticed in an app pop-up by the folks over at Android Authority earlier this week. It’s also live on a Google support page where the company explains:

	

Photos and videos that you delete will stay in your trash for 30 days before they are permanently deleted. Photos and videos that were permanently deleted can’t be restored.

That previously read as 60 days, with the change apparently being effective as of September 4, 2026, according to archived versions of that page. Just a day prior, it still read as 60 days.

title: Motorola’s wide Razr Fold wants to have ‘3D glass’ and a creaseless display
snippet: The puzzle pieces for the Motorola wide Razr Fold are slowly coming together. A recent World Power Consortium listing for the device, along with leaked internal mockups from Motorola’s design team, more or less cements a Wide Razr Fold in the works to take on the Galaxy Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
The puzzle pieces for the Motorola wide Razr Fold are slowly coming together. A recent World Power Consortium listing for the device, along with leaked internal mockups from Motorola’s design team, more or less cements a Wide Razr Fold in the works to take on the Galaxy Fold 8 and iPhone Duo.

Earlier this month, we obtained internal concept images of what’s very likely the Motorola Razr Fold Wide, though it probably won’t go by that name. They were never published because we didn’t feel there was sufficient supporting evidence at the time. There was no teaser from Motorola at the time, though the images we obtained contained watermarks from Lenovo/Motorola. Those are key to why we’re now posting these.

Motorola’s concept sketches show off a surprising amount of detail. For instance, portions of the mockup are backed by descriptions like “bezel-less” and “3D glass,” referring to the cover display. The latter descriptor sits next to a drawing of a Razr, not the Fold. It still may refer to a new push for a different cover display panel. It’s possible “3D glass” refers to curved screen edges similar to what we often see on the Motorola Edge series.

It also looks like Motorola wants to get closer to Apple’s design philosophy with a bezel-less front display, even with sharp left corners and rounded right edges. Without a bezel, the cover display would have to have the same look as the iPhone Duo. The other option is something like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which uses bezels to soften the harsh corners on the left of the screen.

	

Another page in the document suggests Motorola wants to get as close as possible to a creaseless display with the wide Razr Fold, as seen plainly written across one of the images. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo get extremely close to this, but not quite. Maybe Motorola has the ability to reduce the inner display’s crease to nothing, maybe it’s just marketing talk. Either way, the existing Razr Fold has a more noticeable crease than most, so there’s plenty of room for improvement.

What makes these leaked images worth noting is that the same watermark is used in WPC listings for Motorola Razr devices. It showed up on the existing Razr Fold’s listing back in April, and what brought this to our attention was a new listing posted this week that’s also for the existing Razr Fold, but a Verizon variant of the device. As of now, that doesn’t exist, but the model number is identical outside of a “V” designation that points to a Verizon variant. This updated model also jumps up to the Qi 2.2.1 standard version, though still without magnets inside.

It’s hard to make any definite assessments around the Razr Fold on Verizon based on this listing alone, but the watermark tells us that the leaked materials are almost certainly a real indicator of what Motorola wants to deliver on its wider Razr Fold release.

title: Xiaomi 18 Fold goes on sale with full specs and a Galaxy Z Fold 8 comparison [Gallery]
snippet: Following an appearance at IFA 2026 last week, Xiaomi has posted the full details of its new wide Fold, while it’s also been directly compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8. more…
fullText:
Following an appearance at IFA 2026 last week, Xiaomi has posted the full details of its new wide Fold, while it’s also been directly compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

Pre-orders for the Xiaomi 18 Fold are now open in China and, with that, a full breakdown of the foldable’s specs. This includes a 5.38-inch outer display, 7.58-inch inner display, as well as the Xiaomi XRing O3 chipset that was previously announced. But, going further down the list, there are some other powerful specs on offer.

A 6,000 mAh battery (with 67W wired charging/50W wireless) powers the show, way bigger than the 4,800 mAh battery in Samsung’s device. That’s despite a clear difference in size. As The Verge shows in a hands-on, Samsung’s wide foldable is both taller and narrower than Xiaomi’s when folded. The same article calls out that Xiaomi’s device has almost the exact aspect ratio as an IMAX display. 

Images via The Verge

Xiaomi’s listing further details the dimensions at 117.8 x 83.6 x 10.68mm when the foldable is closed, opening up to 163.8mm wide and 5.02mm thick when unfolded. Storage and memory options range from 12GB + 256GB up to 16GB + 1TB. 

	

The triple camera array around back includes a 200MP main sensor, 50MP 3.5x telephoto, and a 50MP ultrawide too. 

Colors include “Warm Gold,” “White,” “Black,” and “Nishino Red” (translated).

There’s also a light pink “Ceramic” model.

The Xiaomi 18 Fold is available for purchase now in China starting at ¥10,999. Directly converted, that’s just shy of $1,640 USD. It’s still unclear if or when this foldable might make its way to global markets, but it’s certainly an intriguing release.

title: Android rolling out passkey transfers between password managers
snippet: Google announced today that Android now offers a system-level way to transfer passwords and passkeys between credential managers. more…
fullText:
Google announced today that Android now offers a system-level way to transfer passwords and passkeys between credential managers.

In the past, transferring credentials between password managers involved “downloading them into an unencrypted text file, which left them unprotected on your device.” Meanwhile, passkeys did not originally offer a transfer method, thus requiring you to manually “recreate them across multiple sites and apps.”

Android wants to solve these issues by offering an operating system-backed transfer method:

Start the move: Open your new password manager app and choose the option to import or copy your passwords and passkeys from another provider. The password manager will then hand the task over to Android.

Let Android securely coordinate the data transfer: Android will automatically detect existing password managers on your device and show you which you can import from.

Review and authorize: Once you tap “Continue,” Android will bring you to your existing password manager to select, review, and authorize the transfer. Then your data will be quickly and securely transferred between the apps in just a few seconds.

The screenshots above show the import flow for Google Password Manager.

	

At launch, the transfer experience is supported by Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Other partners can participate by supporting the Credential Manager’s Credentials Transfer API.

title: Annoyingly, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the best advert for an iPhone Fold yet
snippet: Samsung has beaten Apple to the punch, but I’m annoyed that while it’s, in fact, a fantastic device, it’ll only help bolster the sales of the long-rumored iPhone Fold. more…
fullText:
Samsung has beaten Apple to the punch, but I’m annoyed that while it’s, in fact, a fantastic device, it’ll only help bolster the sales of the long-rumored iPhone Fold.

It is a really ironic position for Samsung to find itself in. They have spent years flexing their engineering muscle, burning through iterations, and pushing folding display technology to its absolute limit to lead this space. Although I would argue that some others are doing the “traditional” foldable better now.

Yet despite all the leading, innovating, and market domination, Samsung’s latest flagship wide-body foldable might just end up courting buyers right into Apple’s hands with its iPhone Fold.

The cynic in me sort of feels that, like the Galaxy S25 Edge, getting ahead of Apple was a calculated play to try and court those who are intrigued by the form factor, but maybe not ready to commit to the very compromised 1:1 aspect-ratio’d Z Folds. It’s hard to argue that most folding phones are narrow devices that feel like holding a thick TV remote when closed.

	

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is refreshing compared to Samsung’s previous folding phones because it’s leaning into the entertainment strengths that are supposedly why folding phones are so popular. As with any tech product, there are always going to be compromises, especially when it’s a 2-in-1 experience. Foldables are mature, but the wide body feels like it’s ready to be fully explored. In my mind, a wide-body folding phone is the optimal design. The final form is the tri-fold, which, coincidentally, Samsung has managed to ship to those with deep enough pockets.

Back to the Fold 8: for the most part, many reviews have pointed out how refreshing the Z Fold 8 is despite the fact that Oppo and Google did it first. Samsung has just done it better than anyone thus far. In fact, the Z Fold 8 is easily one of my favorite smartphones of the last few years. As soon as I picked it up, it made sense. I carry it as a secondary phone with a backup SIM. It is my Balatro-playing, web-scrolling, book-reading, movie-watching phone. It’s a small tablet, but also a small phone; there’s literally nothing to hate in my mind.

It probably doesn’t help that Samsung grapples with a fundamentally different challenge than Apple. Samsung is forced to lead the space, combat a wave of aggressive Chinese competitors, and constantly prove why it deserves to be the king of Android hardware. It has to innovate in public, iterate openly, and deal with the early design missteps that come with pioneering new categories.

When everyday people see the Z Fold 8 in public or read reviews praising its new wide-body format, they don’t necessarily think about switching to Android. Instead, they think, “If a folding phone can finally look and feel this good, I can’t wait to see what Apple does with an iPhone Fold.” Samsung is doing all the heavy lifting of educating the public and legitimizing the form factor, only for Apple to potentially reap the rewards.

Cards on the table, I do not like iOS, but I’m under no illusions that Apple will have optimized every single aspect of the experience to maximize the experience on the inner and outer screen. Android’s foldable software has improved significantly over the years, but app optimization across varying aspect ratios on Android remains a hit-or-miss affair depending on whether developers care to update their apps. I’m having a great time, but some things could be better. Apple doesn’t have that problem—when Apple drops a new form factor, developers fall in line almost immediately.

We might have differing opinions on our mobile OS of choice, but 9to5Mac’s own Fernando Silva had some very positive things to say about the wider Galaxy Z Fold 8. While we’ve had folding devices for almost a decade, it’s interesting to see the critiques from an Apple-centric position. I implore you to go check it out.

In hindsight, the iPad Mini was the very first step ahead of a potential iPhone Fold. It’s a compact tablet running iPadOS with multi-window capabilities tailored for small-format tablet displays. The second step was the ultra-thin design language introduced with the iPhone Air. Apple’s undoubted prowess in the tablet space has likely held back some internal ambitions to ship a folding phone. They didn’t want to cannibalize their own iPad Mini sales until the market was mature enough to justify merging those two product lines. The tech market is mature now, so for Apple, it’s clearly time to enter the space.

When an iPhone user looks at a Galaxy Z Fold 8, they see an incredible piece of engineering, but they also see One UI, a different app ecosystem, and a departure from their comfort zone. Instead of acting as a gateway to convert those users to Samsung, the Z Fold 8 serves as a proof of concept.

It proves to the “average user” – a phrase I’m not all that fond of – that folding phones are no longer delicate, awkward experiments with annoying aspect ratios. It reassures them that the hardware is ready, leaving them content to simply wait for Apple to drop its own version. Samsung has built a fantastic device that, annoyingly, has accidentally become the ultimate marketing campaign for Apple’s next big thing.

title: Oppo confirms Find X10 Pro Max and its triple 200MP camera setup will launch this month
snippet: As it gears up for launch later this month, Oppo has teased the Find X10 Pro Max with its new addition to the lineup and a triple 200MP camera setup that sounds a bit insane. more…
fullText:
As it gears up for launch later this month, Oppo has teased the Find X10 Pro Max with its new addition to the lineup and a triple 200MP camera setup that sounds a bit insane.

In a post on Weibo, Oppo teases that the Find X10 Pro Max will be the “most powerful” device in its class in regards to imaging this year, and it certainly sounds like it.

As rumored, the post confirms that the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max will come with not one, not two, but three 200MP cameras around back. The main sensor has “DeepPix technology” along with improvements to dynamic range and stabilization, all while managing f/1.5 aperture for increased light capture. The 200MP ultrawide shooter features a 124-degree field-of-view and f/2.2 aperture. The telephoto camera, finally, pairs its 200MP sensor with even better stabilization compared to the main sensor, f/2.1 aperture, and has macro capabilities. The only thing not mentioned is the optical zoom. 

All three cameras can capture in 8K, the post mentions. 

	

It sounds wild, and we’ll find out more soon as the Find X10 series is now confirmed to be launching in September, and more teasers are also set to drop in the coming days, too, the post teases.
